feed.title: Debezium
feed.subtitle: Debezium is an open source distributed platform for change data capture. Start it up, point it at your databases, and your apps can start responding to all of the inserts, updates, and deletes that other apps commit to your databases. Debezium is durable and fast, so your apps can respond quickly and never miss an event, even when things go wrong.

entry.title: Single Sign-On for the Debezium Platform

link.title: Single Sign-On for the Debezium Platform

entry.content:
Identity and Access Management is a highly anticipated feature for the Debezium Platform, slatted for Q4.

Until then, we can explore what is currently possible: Single Sign-on, OpenID Connect, and even brokering Entra ID. In this first post, I will walk you through putting a Debezium Platform deployment on Kubernetes behind a single sign-on (SSO) login with Keycloak as an Identity Provider.

The scenario throughout the blog series is Contoso Retail, a fictional company on the domain contoso.com, running the Platform on a Kubernetes cluster and wanting its own staff list to govern access to it. Contoso Retail uses Entra ID as its corporate directory.

This works thanks to a PR I authored. But as is often the case with OSS contributions, my work rests on the shoulders of giants: the conductor, the Platform’s API, is a Java Quarkus application, and Quarkus has excellent support for OIDC — most of the hard part was already done.

As I will show, the Debezium Platform doesn’t care if your organization uses Entra ID, Amazon Cognito, Okta, etc. An OAuth2 proxy intercepts the request to the Platform and hands you to Keycloak, whose login page carries an SSO button for the third-party identity provider (Entra ID, for example) with all its capabilities — 2FA, geolocation, and other conditional-access policies. Keycloak then brokers that corporate directory information: it mints ID and access tokens compliant with OIDC by mapping the identity and authorization information it receives.

Getting there takes three steps, one per post:

  • This post — a working login. The Kubernetes deployment, with oauth2-proxy in front and Keycloak as the identity provider behind it — no brokering to Entra ID yet.

  • The second — a real corporate directory. Replacing the hand-made Keycloak users by brokering to Microsoft Entra ID, so that user lifecycle and group membership live where the organization already manages them.

  • The third — laying the groundwork for RBAC. The difference between an ID token and an access token, and how to get roles into the correct token.

A word on scope

In his mid-year update post, Mario highlights the exciting coming features for the platform, including Identity and Access Management (IAM).

This series of posts is an experiment that precedes the final architecture. It focuses on Single Sign-On (SSO) using the OpenID Connect (OIDC) protocol. Two tokens will be issued by Keycloak, the platform’s identity provider (IdP): an ID token (who are you — authentication) and an access token (what claims are you entitled to — authorization). At the time of writing, the Debezium Platform does not enforce roles defined in the access token.

Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) and other critical points of the security architecture are currently being worked on. I encourage readers to subscribe to the Debezium blog for exciting announcements on the IAM implementation progress.

All the host names in this post are Contoso’s, but the lab behind them ran on a domain I own, 1int.io — which is what the screenshots and decoded tokens actually show: demo.1int.io where the text says demo.contoso.com. Nothing about that domain is special. Anyone with a domain name of their own can reproduce all of it.

Two things are genuinely required:

  • A machine with a public IPv4 address, and a domain whose DNS you can point at it. Two A records under a sub-zone of your own choosing, which is where section 2 starts. The posts rely on valid TLS certificates, and a Let’s Encrypt DNS-01 challenge proves you own the zone by writing a record into it — so the name has to be genuinely yours.

  • A Microsoft Entra ID account — for the next post in this series, so it can wait a short while. An Azure free trial or a pay-as-you-go subscription both produce a usable tenant, and everything that post does — app registrations, app roles, users, groups — is Entra ID Free, so the lab itself costs nothing to run.

Why not a self-signed certificate?

Because the browser is not the only client, and it is the only one with a "proceed anyway" button.

A self-signed certificate is still HTTPS, and you can click through the browser’s warning. However, two of the exchanges in this post never involve a browser at all: oauth2-proxy resolves OIDC discovery against Keycloak at startup and trades the authorization code for tokens on every login, and the conductor fetches the realm’s public keys to validate every bearer it is handed. Those clients are a Go binary and a JVM. Neither has a warning to click through; both just fail the handshake.

Entra ID arrives in the second post with a rule of its own — a redirect URI must never be plain HTTP — but a self-signed certificate satisfies that one. It is the two calls above that rule it out, and they are already here in this post.

Working around it means installing your CA into each trust store independently: the JVM’s for the conductor, the container’s bundle for oauth2-proxy, and every browser and operating system that will ever open the UI. That is more work than the DNS-01 challenge it replaces, and it has to be repeated for every component you add.

  • 1. Getting started

  • 2. DNS first, because everything else waits on it

  • 3. The proxy config, and how it relates to the IdP

  • 4. The actual Kubernetes deployment for the Debezium Platform

  • 5. One proxy, two clients

1. Getting started

Deploying the Debezium platform is simple and well-documented. Deploying it with support for SSO becomes substantially more complicated. Every piece of the deployment is an ordinary Helm chart, and you are welcome to install them by hand. But there are over 10 of them, and they have to go in a particular order. To ensure the platform I am demonstrating is quality-controlled by a CI and thoroughly exercised, I am using debezium-platform-lab, a companion repository that stands the whole stack up.

It is there purely as a convenience, and nothing in this post depends on it. Feel free to use it as a reference guide by checking out the docs. And if you want to reproduce the exact setup I used for this blog, read the Hetzner guide.

It is a community project. Not affiliated with, or endorsed by, the Debezium project or Commonhaus Foundation.

This post was written against v0.3.0. If main has since moved on, that tag is the state described here.

What you need

Whether using the companion repo or doing it yourself, you need five things.

  • A Kubernetes cluster. 8 GB of RAM comfortably covers what this post deploys — the Platform, monitoring, and the identity chain of Keycloak, its database and oauth2-proxy, of which only Keycloak is a JVM. Nodes must be amd64 — the Platform release images have no other architecture, nightly aside.

  • The Debezium Platform — stage, its UI, and the conductor, its API.

  • oauth2-proxy — the reverse proxy that fronts the platform host and holds the session.

  • Keycloak — the identity provider that issues the tokens, and later brokers to Entra ID.

  • Tooling, on your workstation rather than the cluster: just, helmfile with helm, and kubectl. The repository’s prerequisites page lists them with install links. k9s is optional and worth having.

Ports 80 and 443 must be reachable from anywhere

Not merely from your own address. An OIDC redirect comes back through whatever browser the user is sitting at, and a cloud firewall defaulting to "my IP only" is the usual thing that breaks it.

The rest of this post reads kubectl output, helm list and k9s constantly.

In my case, the lab is running on a Hetzner Cloud VM running k3s, with DNS at Gandi. To reinforce the case: it does not matter. Any machine with a public IPv4 address works — EC2, a droplet, bare metal in a cupboard — and any registrar with an API works for the DNS.

Where a command below is provider-specific it is called out, along with what the equivalent looks like elsewhere.

2. DNS first, because everything else waits on it

Take the public IPv4 address of the machine you provisioned and point a name at it. The zone has to exist and be yours before cert-manager can do anything: a Let’s Encrypt DNS-01 challenge proves ownership by writing a TXT record into it, so you will need to obtain API credentials from whoever hosts your DNS. The A records are what make the platform reachable once the certificate exists.

I recommend giving the lab a sub-zone of its own. Two advantages: no risk of collision if contoso.com already does something, and everything is nicely scoped under demo.*.

demo.contoso.com      A   <public-ip>
*.demo.contoso.com    A   <public-ip>

If following the guide in the companion repo, set DPL_DOMAIN=demo.contoso.com, and the platform publishes auth.demo.contoso.com and dmp.demo.contoso.com. Two records, one throwaway branch of your zone, and nothing that already works stops working.

One naming trap

For those following the guide, do not make the sub-zone dmp.. The platform publishes its UI at dmp.${DPL_DOMAIN}, so DPL_DOMAIN=dmp.contoso.com gets you dmp.dmp.contoso.com. Pick a label that names the environment — demo, lab2, sso — not one that names a component.

At Gandi

Their DNS product is LiveDNS, and records are named relative to the zone. The zone is still contoso.com; the two record names are demo and *.demo.

In the web console: Domain → DNS Records → Add record, type A, name demo, then again with name *.demo.

Everywhere else

The concept ports exactly; only the tool changes.

Provider Equivalent

Route 53

aws route53 change-resource-record-sets with an UPSERT batch, or the console

Cloudflare

POST /zones/<id>/dns_records, or flarectl dns create

Google Cloud DNS

gcloud dns record-sets update <name> --type=A --rrdatas=<ip>

Anything else

Two A records under a sub-zone. Every registrar can do this.

For the certificate step later, the only thing that matters is whether cert-manager has a DNS-01 solver for your provider. It ships built-in solvers for Route 53, Cloud DNS, Cloudflare and a handful of others; Gandi is not among them, which is why that part of the lab runs an out-of-tree webhook. If your DNS lives at one of the built-ins, that section gets simpler rather than harder. Just remember to use the shortest TTL possible for the records, so the propagation is as fast as possible.

Check it before moving on

$ dig +short demo.contoso.com
203.0.113.10  # should be your IPv4 public address
$ dig +short auth.demo.contoso.com
203.0.113.10

The second one is the one that matters — it is answered by the wildcard, and it is what every component host depends on. You can also run dig +short anything.contoso.com to make sure everything is contained to demo or whatever you chose. It should return nothing.

Why not sslip.io

Wildcard DNS services like sslip.io and nip.io resolve 203-0-113-10.sslip.io to 203.0.113.10 with no configuration at all, but they are useless here. Let’s Encrypt will not issue for them, and DNS-01 needs a zone you can write to.

And downstream of both: Entra ID rejects any redirect URI that is not HTTPS, with only localhost exempt. So the whole single-sign-on path depends on a real certificate, which depends on a real zone. This is the step that decides whether the rest of the post is possible — which is why it comes first.

But enough about DNS, on to the actual SSO setup.

3. The proxy config, and how it relates to the IdP

Everything that follows rests on one file: the configuration of the oauth2-proxy instance that fronts the platform host. It is short but well worth reading closely because most of its values are critical to a secured OIDC flow and depend on Keycloak’s settings.

An important concept related to Keycloak is that of a realm. It will be mentioned several times going forward. A Keycloak realm is a self-contained identity domain — its own users, roles, clients and signing keys — so an account in one realm does not exist as far as another is concerned.

Below is the file as I configured it in the companion repo, with its comments stripped.

config:
  existingSecret: oauth2-proxy-secret
  configFile: |-
    provider = "oidc"
    oidc_issuer_url = "https://auth.demo.contoso.com/realms/dmp"
    redirect_url = "https://dmp.demo.contoso.com/oauth2/callback"
    email_domains = ["*"]
    insecure_oidc_allow_unverified_email = true
    cookie_domains = [".demo.contoso.com"]
    cookie_secure = true
    cookie_refresh = "4m"
    cookie_expire = "10h"
    whitelist_domains = [".demo.contoso.com"]
    reverse_proxy = true
    pass_authorization_header = true
    pass_access_token = true
    skip_provider_button = true
    upstreams = [
      "http://conductor.dmp.svc.cluster.local:8080/api/",
      "http://stage.dmp.svc.cluster.local:3000/"
    ]

extraArgs:
  code-challenge-method: S256

ingress:
  enabled: true
  className: traefik
  path: /
  pathType: Prefix
  hosts:
    - dmp.demo.contoso.com
  tls:
    - secretName: wildcard-demo-contoso-com-tls
      hosts:
        - dmp.demo.contoso.com

The upstreams are the interesting structural part. /api/ goes to the conductor and everything else to stage, which is what makes this a reverse proxy rather than an authentication side-car. Note the trailing slash on /api/: it makes the match a subtree. Without it the match is exact, /api/pipelines falls through to the / upstream, and the stage UI answers an API call with HTML.

skip_provider_button removes the "Sign in with…" since there is exactly one provider: Keycloak.

The realm is the source of truth

The values that govern time are not free variables. Keycloak decides them, and the proxy either agrees or behaves incoherently. Realm settings → Sessions:

and Realm settings → Tokens:

Four numbers on those two screens determine how the proxy has to be configured to avoid a slew of 401 errors while still appearing to have a browser session:

Keycloak realm setting Value What it forces

Access Token Lifespan

5 minutes

The proxy must renew its access token more often than this

SSO Session Idle

30 minutes

After 30 minutes of inactivity the refresh token is dead and the user logs in again

SSO Session Max

10 hours

A hard ceiling: no proxy session should outlive it

Revoke Refresh Token

Disabled

A refresh token can be used multiple times

Keycloak even states the relationship on screen — "It is recommended for this value to be shorter than the SSO session idle timeout: 30 minutes".

Correct OIDC behavior

An oauth2-proxy session holds the access token it received at login. It does not renew that token unless told to, and the setting that tells it is cookie_refresh — disabled by default. So with a 5-minute access token, the proxy hands the conductor a token that is valid for five minutes and then indefinitely stale, and the conductor rejects it. The user sees a UI that loads perfectly while every API call fails, because the stage SPA component is unaware of any OIDC setup — remember, the proxy fronts it.

The other half is cookie_expire, which defaults to 168 hours. Against an SSO Session Max of 10 hours, that is a proxy session widely outliving the identity session it was derived from.

Which is where the two lines already in the config above come from:

# Renew before the 5-minute access token expires.
cookie_refresh = "4m"
# Do not outlive SSO Session Max.
cookie_expire = "10h"

This is worth remembering: the identity provider owns the various TTLs.

4. The actual Kubernetes deployment for the Debezium Platform

The platform deploys on Kubernetes, so let’s briefly discuss some important information pertaining to it.

As indicated before, you can install the entire setup yourself — though not everything in that list is required for just an SSO login. The companion repo provides a just recipe that resolves the whole helmfile and prints the release list without touching the cluster:

$ just platform-sso-releases
just releases --state-values-file examples/k3s/platform-sso/components.yaml
cert-manager
cert-manager-webhook-gandi
dns01-gandi
cnpg-operator
debezium-platform
keycloak
keycloak-db
keycloak-operator
oauth2-proxy
kafka-cluster
strimzi-cluster-operator
kube-prometheus-stack
opentelemetry-operator

just apply and it deploys correctly, respecting ordering and dependencies — more on that later.

A reality check

Single sign-on here covers the Debezium Platform and nothing else: one host, behind one proxy. Everything else in the list is left as an exercise for the reader.

Orchestrating single sign-on across an entire stack is that same work repeated per component: a client registration and a redirect URI for each, a proxy in front of anything that cannot speak OIDC itself, and a decision about the ones that can do neither. Single sign-on is not a component you install, it is a property that only holds where every component in scope has been made to agree.

Also worth noting is that I am running the platform on k3s, so there is no ingress controller in the release since k3s bundles Traefik.

That list is alphabetical, but the order is not

Each release declares what it needs:

  - name: keycloak
    namespace: identity
    needs:
      - identity/keycloak-operator
      - identity/keycloak-db

Helmfile takes every one of those edges, builds a DAG, and runs each layer concurrently. So the real answer to "in what order" is four waves:

Read left to right, three independent chains run side by side and only converge at the end:

  • Certificates — cert-manager, then the letsencrypt-prod ClusterIssuer that dispatches to it.

  • Kafka — the Strimzi operator, then the Kafka custom resource it reconciles. Not strictly required, but what is the fun of deploying an empty Debezium platform?

  • Identity — the Keycloak operator and a CloudNativePG database in parallel, both required before Keycloak itself.

The last wave is the one that fails

Wave 4 is oauth2-proxy, and on a first run it will not deploy. It needs an OIDC client secret from a Keycloak realm that won’t exist until wave 3 is finished, and we log in to Keycloak to start configuring SSO.

Here is the identity namespace at the end of the first pass:

That is the graph doing its job, and the red line is worth reading closely rather than skipping past.

Everything the proxy depends on is up: Keycloak, its CloudNativePG database, and the operator that reconciled them, all 1/1 Running. Only the last wave is red — and the status is specific. CreateContainerConfigError is not a crash and not a failed health check: it narrows the issue to a referenced ConfigMap or Secret missing, or to missing required values inside them. The container was never started at all, because kubelet could not assemble its environment: the Secret holding the OIDC client ID does not exist yet. Note the restart count, still 0. Nothing is looping, nothing is burning CPU retrying, and there are no application logs to go and read, because no application ever ran. So the helm release is a success:

5. One proxy, two clients

Here is every Secret in the identity namespace after the first pass:

No oauth2-proxy-secret yet. Nothing is going to create it: it is the one part of this deployment that cannot be generated, because its contents do not exist until a human has registered a client in Keycloak.

Hands on Keycloak…​ finally

Of the entries that are there keycloak-initial-admin contains the first admin account credentials generated by the Keycloak operator. To read it, use your favorite Kubernetes admin tool, or simply in a terminal, one command for the username, once for the password:

kubectl -n identity get secret keycloak-initial-admin \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d
kubectl -n identity get secret keycloak-initial-admin \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.username}' | base64 -d

Log in at https://auth.demo.contoso.com with those credentials.

First, a permanent admin

The account you just pulled out of that Secret is a bootstrap credential. Keycloak calls it a temporary admin and logs a warning about it on every startup; the operator generates it so that there is some way in on a fresh install, not so that you keep using it. Replace it before doing anything else.

It lives in master — Keycloak’s own realm, the one that administers the server itself. The permanent admin belongs in master as well, so stay where you are rather than switching realms for this.

Users → Add user. Username, email, first and last name.

Credentials → Set password, and turn Temporary to Off.

That toggle defaults to On, which marks the password as already expired and forces a change at next login.

Role mapping → Assign role → Realm Roles → admin.

default-roles-master comes with every new account; admin is the one that matters, and with Hide inherited roles ticked you can see it was granted directly rather than picked up from a group.

Sign out of the console from the user menu in the top right, then sign back in at the same URL as the new account rather than the bootstrap one:

https://auth.demo.contoso.com/admin/master/console/

Once that works, the bootstrap account has done its job and can go: Users → temp-admin → Delete. The startup warning goes with it.

The next step is to create a realm for the Debezium Platform. Manage realms → Create realm and name it dmp.

Since everything the platform authenticates against lives in dmp, click on it so you can start configuring it.

Configuring our first Keycloak client

Authorization code flow with Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) is a mouthful. I will leave it as an exercise for the reader to learn more about it here. There are many good tutorials out there as well.

In summary: oauth2-proxy sends you to Keycloak to log in, Keycloak sends you back carrying a one-time ticket (the code) and oauth2-proxy redeems that ticket for your tokens in a direct conversation the browser never sees.

PKCE adds one guarantee on top: before sending you off, the application (oauth2-proxy) invents a secret and hands over only a fingerprint of it. Redeeming the ticket requires producing the original. So a ticket stolen in transit is worthless to whoever took it. Since RFC 9700 (OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice) it’s recommended for all clients using the authorization code flow.

The second post in this series adds one hop: Keycloak stops checking the password itself and forwards you to Entra ID, then brokers what comes back.

Creating it

A Keycloak client is a registration bound to a set of valid redirect URIs, and that binding is the load-bearing security control in the whole flow.

Clients → Create client, then:

  • Client ID: oauth2-proxy — the proxy sends it as client_id, so a typo here surfaces later as invalid_client.

  • Client authentication: On. This makes it a confidential client, which is what generates the secret the proxy needs. Left off, the client is public, there is no Credentials tab, and there is nothing to put in the Kubernetes Secret.

  • Standard flow enabled. That is authorization-code, the flow in the diagram above.

  • Valid redirect URIs: https://dmp.demo.contoso.com/oauth2/callback

Then Credentials → Client secret → copy. That value goes into Kubernetes next, and Keycloak will show it again later, so there is no need to be precious about it.

Require PKCE is On, with PKCE Method S256. That is the Keycloak half of the code-challenge-method: S256 line in the values file from section 3, and the two halves have to agree. Turn it on here while the proxy is not sending a challenge and every login dies at the authorization request with invalid_request: Missing parameter: code_challenge_method — so set the proxy side first if you are enabling it on a running deployment.

The second client, which nobody redirects to

The conductor expects a client named conductor as well. It never appears in the flow above, because it never logs anybody in — it validates tokens rather than issuing them, running as a Quarkus OIDC resource server. No redirect URI, no callback, no browser involvement. It is strictly needed by the conductor (a resource server in OIDC parlance) as its own entry in the dmp realm, and will carry the RBAC configuration — out of scope for now.

Handing the credentials back to Kubernetes

Feed the secret you copied from Keycloak above to Kubernetes:

kubectl -n identity create secret generic oauth2-proxy-secret \
  --from-literal=client-id=oauth2-proxy \
  --from-literal=client-secret='<from Keycloak>' \
  --from-literal=cookie-secret="$(openssl rand -base64 24)"

The cookie-secret has nothing to do with Keycloak. It is the key the proxy uses to encrypt its own session cookie, so it is generated locally and never leaves the cluster.

Pass two

If using the companion repo just platform-sso, otherwise re-apply the oauth2-proxy Helm release.

The proxy finds its Secret, starts, resolves OIDC discovery against https://auth.demo.contoso.com/realms/dmp, and goes Ready:

A user to log in with

Everything is running, and nobody can log in.

The administrator from earlier lives in master. The proxy authenticates against /realms/dmp, so that account is not merely unprivileged at the platform’s login form — it is invisible to it. Keycloak will not find it because it is not looking in that realm.

This is the realm boundary paying off exactly as advertised a few paragraphs ago. Nobody had to remember to withhold platform access from the administrator. The two populations are separate because they live in different realms, and the proxy only ever asks about one of them.

Let’s add our first user to the dmp realm:

Users → Add user, in dmp:

  • Fill in all four fields: username, email, first name, last name.

    The email is what oauth2-proxy uses to build a session. email_domains = ["*"] accepts any domain, but not a missing one — so a user without an email authenticates against Keycloak perfectly and is then rejected by the proxy.

    First and last name are required by the realm’s user profile — though Keycloak would prompt you for that information upon your first login attempt.

  • Email verified on or off. The proxy sets insecure_oidc_allow_unverified_email = true anyway.

  • Credentials → Set password → Temporary: Off, exactly as before.

  • No role mappings: RBAC is out-of-scope for now, so any authenticated user in the dmp realm has full access to the Debezium platform.

The first login

Finally, the reward for all our efforts!

https://dmp.demo.contoso.com

No /login path — the proxy owns the entire host, so any URL under it starts the flow. The round trip is the one from the diagram earlier: a 302 to Keycloak, the realm’s sign-in form, back to /oauth2/callback with a code, a code-for-tokens exchange the browser never sees, a session cookie scoped to dmp.demo.contoso.com, and then:

Look at the address bar first: dmp.demo.contoso.com, clean. No ?code=, no /oauth2/callback. The proxy consumed the callback, exchanged the code, set its cookie and sent the browser on to the path originally asked for. The entire round trip leaves no trace in the URL, which is exactly what you want.

Missing in the stage interface: a user menu, an account name, a sign-out button. At the time of this writing, stage does not know it is behind an identity provider. As far as it is concerned, every request has simply arrived, exactly as it did before any of this existed. The goal is stage speaking OIDC natively, at which point this front door stops being necessary.

OIDC in action behind the scenes

That "Welcome to Stage" screen is doing more work than it looks like.

A rendered page, on its own, proves only that the proxy let the request through — the SPA shell is served by stage and would render regardless. What makes this screen evidence is that stage immediately calls the conductor at /api/, and the conductor is an OIDC resource server: it validates the bearer token on every request against the realm’s JWKS.

  • oauth2-proxy matched /api/ as a subtree and routed it to conductor:8080, while everything else went to stage:3000.

  • pass_authorization_header injected Authorization: Bearer <access_token> into the upstream request — not the auth response, which is the distinction that makes reverse-proxy mode work where forward-auth would not.

  • The conductor fetched the realm’s JWKS from https://auth.demo.contoso.com — a server-to-server call, with no browser to click a warning through — and validated the signature.

  • It answered 200 with an empty pipeline list, which is what the welcome screen is.

"No pipelines yet" is a successful API response. Had any link in that chain broken, the page would have loaded and then failed: a spinner, an error panel, or a blank frame where the pipeline list should be. Which is precisely why the empty state, and not the page loading, is the proof.

Where the session actually lives

Worth noting that the proxy holds a cookie of its own, scoped to the zone the platform lives in, encrypted with its own cookie secret — seen here in a browser developer console:

What that cookie is derived from sits one layer up: Keycloak’s own session, held as a cookie on auth.demo.contoso.com. When the proxy redirected there, Keycloak decided whether the user was already authenticated, and returned an authorization code without asking again if they were. The proxy then ran its own code exchange and minted its own independent cookie.

The private window is the control that proves it. Same URL, same proxy, same everything except a browser profile carrying no Keycloak cookie — and the login form appears. Nothing about the platform changed; the only thing missing was the session at the identity provider.

Two things follow, and they are the reason to build it this way:

  • Revocation works. End the session in Keycloak and access is gone at the next redirect. A cookie the application minted for itself would keep working until it expired.

  • It scales past one host. Putting a second UI behind its own proxy means registering a second client, not widening a cookie’s reach — and that second host inherits the same Keycloak session, so the user is not asked to log in twice.

The sign-on is single. The sessions, deliberately, are not.

What is next

You have a login, and that is genuinely the hard half of the plumbing. However, we still need to address two shortcomings.

The users live in Keycloak, typed in by hand, and no organization wants to maintain a second staff list there. The next post fixes that, brokering Keycloak to Microsoft Entra ID so that accounts, group membership and offboarding stay where they already are.

Any account in the realm reaches everything. The last post lays that groundwork — the two tokens Keycloak issues and what each is for, then the client roles, groups and claim path that any future enforcement will rest on.
entry.summary: Identity and Access Management is a highly anticipated feature for the Debezium Platform, slatted for Q4. Until then, we can explore what is currently possible: Single Sign-on, OpenID Connect, and even brokering Entra ID. In this first post, I will walk you through putting a Debezium Platform deployment on Kubernetes behind a single sign-on (SSO) login with Keycloak as an Identity Provider. The scenario throughout the blog series is Contoso Retail, a fictional company on the domain contoso.com, running the Platform on a Kubernetes cluster and wanting its own staff list to govern access to it. Contoso Retail uses Entra ID as its corporate directory.

entry.title: Debezium 3.7.0.Beta1 Released
entry.content:
As summer continues, we’re excited to announce the release of Debezium 3.7.0.Beta1, bringing a broad set of improvements across connectors, Debezium Server, and the Platform UI.

Among the highlights, incremental snapshots now work on PostgreSQL read-only replicas, and Debezium Server gains a new Databricks ZeroBus Ingest sink for direct change event delivery to Unity Catalog-managed Delta tables. This release also includes performance and snapshot optimizations, new connector capabilities, and numerous bug fixes across the board.

Read on for the full details!

  • New features and improvements

  • Other changes

New Features and Improvements

The following covers all new features and improvements, grouped by connector component area.

Debezium for MySQL

Debezium for Oracle

Debezium for PostgreSQL

Debezium JDBC sink

Debezium Platform

Debezium Server

Debezium for CockroachDB

Container Images

Debezium for MySQL

Support for NOBLOB binlog_row_image format

Debezium now supports the NOBLOB binlog row image format for MySQL. This format is commonly used in databases with large BLOB columns that are updated infrequently, as it reduces binlog size by excluding BLOB and TEXT columns from row images when they are not modified. Previously, the connector rejected this format at startup, forcing users to choose between FULL and MINIMAL row image modes.

This behavior is conceptually similar to how PostgreSQL handles unchanged TOAST columns and how Oracle handles LOB values. In all three cases, the database’s replication stream may omit large-value columns that were not modified in a given transaction. During snapshots, all column values are always available because Debezium reads the full row directly via SQL. During streaming, however, when a BLOB or TEXT column was not changed and is therefore excluded from the binlog row image, Debezium populates the field with the configured unavailable.value.placeholder value. This is the same approach used for unavailable TOASTed columns in PostgreSQL and LOB columns in Oracle, giving users a consistent way to detect and handle missing column values across all three databases. (dbz#473)

Debezium for Oracle

Support for BC (negative) timestamps

The Oracle connector now correctly captures dates in the BC era (negative years) across all four Oracle temporal types: DATE, TIMESTAMP, TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, and TIMESTAMP WITH LOCAL TIME ZONE. Previously, a date such as -2018-03-27 inserted via TO_DATE('-2018-03-27', 'SYYYY-MM-DD') would be incorrectly represented as the positive-year equivalent 2018-03-27.

Because Oracle’s calendar has no year zero while ISO 8601 does, BC years are offset by one: Oracle year 2018 BC becomes ISO year -2017. How BC values appear in change events depends on the time.precision.mode setting. Epoch-based types such as io.debezium.time.Timestamp and io.debezium.time.MicroTimestamp emit negative epoch values, while string-based types such as io.debezium.time.ZonedTimestamp emit ISO 8601 strings with a negative year (e.g., "-2017-03-27T01:34:56.007890-11:00").

Both snapshot and streaming paths are covered, and no new connector configuration properties are required. (dbz#1286)

BC values stored in TIMESTAMP(7-9) columns exceed the representable range of io.debezium.time.NanoTimestamp, so users with BC data at nanosecond precision should use time.precision.mode set as isostring or structured only.

LogMiner DML parser performance improvements

The LogMiner DML parser has been significantly optimized, delivering 1.7x to 2.6x higher throughput for UPDATE statement parsing across a range of table widths and column sizes. For tables with wide VARCHAR2 columns or extended 32K strings, the improvements are even more dramatic.

Users who enable the extended MAX_STRING_SIZE parameter may encounter a LogMiner bug where apostrophes in text column values are not properly escaped. Debezium’s relaxed quote detection mode addresses this Oracle limitation, but previously suffered from O(n^2) performance loss for such columns, compounded by text length. This release improves that mode by up to 94x in worst-case scenarios.

These improvements directly translate to higher event throughput for Oracle connectors processing tables with many columns or large column values. (dbz#2491)

The JMH Benchmarks for these changes can be found here.

Debezium for PostgreSQL

Incremental snapshots on read-only replicas

Incremental snapshots on PostgreSQL read-only replicas previously failed with cannot execute pg_current_xact_id() during recovery error, because the snapshot logic attempted to create a new transaction ID, which is not permitted on replicas. This caused connectors running with read.only=true to enter an infinite restart loop when an incremental snapshot was triggered.

This has been corrected, and users running against a hot standby can now use incremental snapshots for re-snapshotting subsets of data without restarting the connector or switching to the primary. (dbz#1080, dbz#2431)

Faster snapshots with per-column type caching

The PostgreSQL connector now caches the resolved column type per ResultSet during snapshots, rather than resolving it on every row. Previously, each row paid the cost of calling ResultSetMetaData.getColumnTypeName and TypeRegistry.get once per column, making overhead scale based on number of columns and rows. For a table with 82 columns, this kept the snapshot producer pinned at around 25K rows per second.

With caching in place, the rowToArray stage runs approximately 35% faster, and end-to-end snapshot throughput for the same table increased to over 30K rows per second. The gain scales with column count and benefits all snapshot flavors, including initial, blocking, incremental, and read-only incremental. (dbz#2350)

Debezium JDBC sink

Opt-in timestamp clamping for out-of-range values

Every database supports a different timestamp range, and Oracle’s BC-era values often fall outside what other databases can represent. The JDBC sink connector introduces timestamp.clamp.out.of.range.values, an opt-in setting that clamps incoming timestamps to the target dialect’s minimum or maximum rather than failing the sink operation. (dbz#1008)

Debezium Platform

Adaptive polling for resource listing pages

The Debezium Platform UI now uses adaptive polling on its resource listing pages. Previously, all listing pages (pipelines, sources, transforms, destinations, and connections) polled data at a fixed 5-second interval, regardless of user activity. The new approach decreases polling frequency when the user is idle and pauses it entirely when the browser tab is in the background, reducing unnecessary API traffic and improving overall UI responsiveness. (dbz#1878)

Connection handling in the pipeline designer

The pipeline designer now handles connections when creating pipelines via Debezium Server configuration. Previously, the flow automatically created sources, destinations, and transforms, but did not manage connection creation. The designer now creates and associates connections with the source and destination configuration, providing a more complete and streamlined pipeline setup experience. (dbz#1906)

Debezium Server

IRSA and WebIdentityToken support for the Kinesis sink

The Kinesis sink now supports AWS IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) and WebIdentityToken-based authentication. Previously, running the Kinesis sink in Kubernetes with a service account mapped to an AWS IAM role failed because the classpath did not include the required AWS STS module. The sink now bundles the software.amazon.awssdk:sts dependency, enabling the default credential provider chain to resolve web identity tokens and assume the target role.

This is especially important for Kubernetes-based deployments on Amazon EKS, where IRSA is the recommended approach for granting AWS permissions to pods without embedding static credentials. (dbz#1738, dbz#2386)

Databricks ZeroBus Ingest sink adapter

Debezium Server now includes a sink adapter for Databricks ZeroBus Ingest, enabling direct change event delivery to Unity Catalog-managed Delta tables without requiring an intermediate message broker. ZeroBus Ingest is Databricks' serverless ingestion API, generally available on AWS and Azure, which writes records directly into managed Delta tables. With this integration, Debezium Server users can set up a streamlined source database to Delta pipeline for change data capture into the Databricks lakehouse.

The sink commits source offsets only after ZeroBus durably writes and acknowledges each batch, providing at-least-once delivery semantics with deterministic idempotency keys. (dbz#2279, dbz#2378)

Correct Prometheus metric labels for sink connectors

The Prometheus JMX Exporter configuration shipped with Debezium Server now correctly labels sink connector metrics. Previously, sink connectors registered their MXBeans with a key ordering that did not match any existing rule pattern. This caused the task key to be embedded inside the name label (e.g., name="jdbc-sink, task=0" instead of name="jdbc-sink" with a separate task="0" label). This broke Prometheus queries, alerts, and dashboards that group or filter by connector name or task ID. (dbz#2380)

Connector profiles for the server distribution

The debezium-server-dist module now includes connector profiles (e.g., connector-postgres, connector-mysql) following the same pattern already present in debezium-server-native-dist. This enables trimmed distribution builds using profile combinations that produce a zip/tar.gz containing only the required connector and sink dependencies.

This is part of an upcoming Debezium feature to support minimal, connector-specific server distributions. More information will be shared in the coming weeks about this new system and how users can take advantage of it. (dbz#2421, dbz#2433)

Debezium for CockroachDB

Schema and table in the source info block

The CockroachDB connector now emits schema and table fields in the source info block of change events, matching the behavior of the PostgreSQL and SQL Server connectors. Previously, the source block carried only db and CockroachDB-specific fields (cluster, resolved_ts, hlc), which blocked JDBC sink topic-to-table routing using collection.name.format templates like ${source.schema}_${source.table}. (dbz#2432)

Optional consumer group offset commits for observability

The CockroachDB connector now supports an opt-in setting to asynchronously commit processed positions to the Kafka consumer group. The connector’s intermediate consumer stores positions in Connect offsets with explicit seeks, which is correct for delivery semantics but makes standard Kafka lag monitoring tools unreliable. For example, kafka-consumer-groups --describe shows no committed offset, and consoles alert on permanently growing lag.

With this option enabled, the connector mirrors its actual progress to the consumer group purely for observability, while correctness continues to rely on Connect offsets. (dbz#2472)

Container Images

PostgreSQL GUC logical decoder support

A recent PostgreSQL security update for PostgreSQL 15 and later introduces a new output_plugin_libraries GUC setting that restricts which logical decoding output plugins can start. By default, PostgreSQL now permits only pgoutput and test_decoding, so any updated PostgreSQL instance, including publicly available container images, will reject the decoderbufs plugin.

The Debezium PostgreSQL container images now explicitly configure this GUC to include decoderbufs alongside the default plugins. For users who have not yet migrated to pgoutput and continue to use decoderbufs, the output_plugin_libraries setting must be specified in the PostgreSQL server configuration to include decoderbufs. (dbz#2434)

Other fixes

  • Incorrect span attribute mapping for type in the Quarkus outbox extension (dbz#2286)

  • Unify include/exclude property validation (dbz#2292)

  • Temporals.max/min give incorrect results for sub-second durations with equal whole seconds (dbz#2338)

  • MathOps.add drops the first operand for BigInteger overloads (dbz#2446)

  • Chunked parallel initial snapshot does not apply snapshot.fetch.size to chunk statements (dbz#2483)

  • timestampOfLSN incorrectly returns the database’s current timestamp (dbz#2162)

  • Schema history record comparator incorrectly evaluates to true on every comparison (dbz#1541)

  • NullPointerException in heartbeat error handlers when the driver reports no SQL state (dbz#2464)

  • Multiple issues in tagged GTID handling (dbz#2496)

  • Upgrade MongoDB driver to 5.9.2 (dbz#2332, dbz#2449)

  • Several MySQL DDL parser fixes for improved statement and identifier handling (dbz#332, dbz#1301, dbz#2381)

  • SQL syntax error on Oracle 11g during boundary queries due to unsupported OFFSET…​FETCH clause (dbz#2448)

  • Username/client filters have no effect when tracking is disabled (dbz#2473)

  • Add ORA-02399 as an allowed Oracle retriable exceptions (dbz#2487)

  • Connector fails to transform column name that is unquoted twice (dbz#1235)

  • Transactional pg_logical_emit_message() events are emitted twice after connector restart (dbz#2004)

  • Connector startup is slow when the database has many custom types (dbz#2041)

  • Snapshot reports serial/bigserial column type while streaming reports int4/int8 (dbz#2232)

  • Incremental snapshot silently loses data on NUMERIC keys holding NaN or Infinity (dbz#2333)

  • Snapshot failure for array values when using the AWS Advanced JDBC driver (dbz#2387)

  • Connector incorrectly parses text defaults containing escaped single quotes (dbz#2440)

  • unavailable.value.placeholder applies to text but not to varchar(max), nvarchar(max), or varbinary(max) (dbz#2420)

  • Upgrade Hibernate to 7.2.19 (dbz#2331)

  • JDBC sink maps propagated SQL Server TINYINT to signed MySQL TINYINT (dbz#2352)

  • JDBC sink cannot write a PostgreSQL numeric[] column that has no type modifier (dbz#2398)

  • JDBC sink omits OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE causing failure on PostgreSQL GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY primary keys (dbz#2459)

  • Upgrade Quarkus to 3.33.2 (dbz#2344)

  • Pulsar OAuth2 private key that is not a data URI is silently truncated instead of rejected (dbz#2395)

  • Failed label is incorrectly shown on the pipeline detail page (dbz#2445)

  • Passwords are not masked in Debezium Server log output (dbz#1201)

  • Connector silently drops cdc=true change events bundled with cdc=false tables in the same mutation (dbz#2388)

  • Changefeed reuse guard ignores paused jobs and creates a duplicate (dbz#2462)

  • Upgrade Kafka to 4.3.1 (dbz#2474)

  • Remove Kafka ConnectorTaskId and LoggingContext dependency from the embedded engine (dbz#2080)

  • JDBC storage RetriableConnection retries a failing operation indefinitely without honoring max.retries (dbz#2244)

In total, 84 issues were resolved in Debezium 3.7.0.Beta1. The list of changes can also be found in our release notes.

entry.title: Debezium 3.7.0.Alpha2 Released
entry.content:
We’re pleased to announce the release of Debezium 3.7.0.Alpha2, the second preview release in the 3.7 series, packed with new features and important changes across the platform.

This release introduces an incubating TiDB connector, adds retry and dead letter queue support for the JDBC sink, and improves Debezium Server with a proper readiness probe. On the Oracle side, the OpenLogReplicator client is now non-blocking and continuous mining for Oracle 12 has been removed. The Debezium Platform UI now surfaces pipeline failures directly, and several other connectors receive important fixes and improvements.

Let’s take a closer look at all these changes and more; read on for the full details!

  • Breaking changes

  • New features and improvements

  • Other changes

Breaking changes

With any new release of software, there can be breaking changes. This release is no exception, so let’s discuss the major changes you should be aware of before upgrading to Debezium 3.7.0.Alpha2

Debezium for Oracle

Continuous mining removed for Oracle 12

Oracle deprecated continuous mining in Oracle 12c and permanently removed it in 19c, and Debezium previously only supported it on a best-effort basis for Oracle 12c deployments. This feature has now been removed entirely from the Oracle connector.

If you are currently using continuous mining with Oracle 12c, you will need to switch to a different capture mode before upgrading. The LogMiner adapter remains the recommended approach for Oracle change data capture. (dbz#1953)

Debezium for Cassandra

Removal of Cassandra 3 connector

Cassandra 3 has reached end of life, and the Cassandra 3 connector has been removed from Debezium. As part of this change, the Guava dependency has been upgraded to version 32.0.0, which is incompatible with Cassandra 3 but aligns with the requirements of Cassandra 4 and later.

If you are currently using the Cassandra 3 connector, you will need to upgrade to Cassandra 4 or later before moving to this release. The Cassandra 4 and Cassandra 5 connectors remain fully supported. (dbz#2273)

New Features and Improvements

The following covers all new features and improvements, grouped by connector component area.

Debezium for Db2

Debezium for MariaDB

Debezium for MySQL

Debezium for Oracle

Debezium for SQL Server

Debezium JDBC sink

Debezium Platform

Debezium Server

Debezium for CockroachDB

Debezium for Informix

TiDB Connector

Debezium AI for Python

Debezium for Db2

LOB column serialization support

The Db2 connector now correctly serializes LOB columns (CLOB, BLOB, and DBCLOB) during both snapshot and streaming. Previously, CLOB and DBCLOB columns emitted internal driver handle strings during snapshots and null values during streaming, while BLOB columns always produced null values.

With this fix, text-based LOB columns are emitted as their string content, and binary LOB columns are serialized according to the configured binary.handling.mode (e.g., base64). (dbz#2304)

Debezium for MariaDB

Support for InnoDB-based binary logs

MariaDB 12.3 introduced a new InnoDB-based binary log storage format designed for improved throughput and crash recovery. The MariaDB connector and binary log client have been updated to ensure compatibility with this new format, allowing Debezium to capture changes from MariaDB deployments that use InnoDB-based binary logging. (dbz#2259)

Correct boolean conversion for negative TINYINT(1) values

The TinyIntOneToBooleanConverter now correctly treats negative TINYINT(1) values as true, matching MySQL’s own semantics where any non-zero value is considered true. Previously, negative values such as -1 or -128 were incorrectly converted to false because the converter used a greater-than-zero check instead of a not-equal-to-zero check. (dbz#2260)

Debezium for MySQL

Correct boolean conversion for negative TINYINT(1) values

The TinyIntOneToBooleanConverter now correctly treats negative TINYINT(1) values as true, matching MySQL’s own semantics where any non-zero value is considered true. Previously, negative values such as -1 or -128 were incorrectly converted to false because the converter used a greater-than-zero check instead of a not-equal-to-zero check. (dbz#2260)

Debezium for Oracle

Non-blocking OpenLogReplicator client

The OpenLogReplicator client has been converted from a blocking to a non-blocking architecture. This improves the responsiveness of connector shutdown operations, as the client can now promptly exit its read loop when a stop is requested rather than waiting for the socket read timeout to expire. (dbz#1198)

Snapshot-only mode no longer requires archive log configuration

The Oracle connector no longer validates archive log destination configuration when running in snapshot-only mode (initial_only). Previously, the archive log validation ran unconditionally at startup, causing snapshot-only runs to fail on managed deployments like Oracle Autonomous Database where the archive log configuration is hidden from the connector user.

This change makes snapshot-only deployments simpler, particularly in cloud-managed Oracle environments where archive log destinations are controlled by the service provider. (dbz#2305)

Debezium for SQL Server

Support for specifying capture instance

The SQL Server connector now allows users to specify which CDC capture instance to use when multiple capture instances exist for the same table. This is useful when different capture instances track different column subsets, preventing unwanted schema changes in downstream topics when a new capture instance is created. (dbz#960)

Debezium JDBC sink

Retry and dead letter queue support

The JDBC sink connector now supports automatic retries with configurable backoff when encountering transient database errors, along with dead letter queue (DLQ) integration for records that fail after all retry attempts. Previously, any SQL exception would immediately stop the sink task, requiring manual intervention to restart.

This makes JDBC sink deployments significantly more resilient in production environments where transient database connectivity issues or constraint violations can occur. (dbz#984)

Sink support for PostgreSQL enum columns

The JDBC sink connector now correctly handles writing to PostgreSQL enum columns. Previously, sinking to a PostgreSQL enum column would fail with a type mismatch error because the generated SQL did not include the necessary type cast. The connector now detects enum column types via the propagated source type metadata and applies the appropriate PostgreSQL cast. (dbz#1344)

Record value and header primary key modes now support deletion

The JDBC sink connector now supports row deletion when using record_value or record_header primary key modes. Previously, deletion was only supported with record_key mode. This provides more flexibility for pipelines where the primary key is derived from the record value or headers rather than the Kafka record key. (dbz#1421)

Debezium Platform

Connection validation for Azure Event Hub

The Debezium Platform now includes a connection validator for Azure Event Hub destinations. This allows users to verify their Event Hub connection settings directly from the Platform UI before creating a pipeline, providing immediate feedback on connectivity issues. (dbz#1088)

Complete CLI platform subsystem

The Debezium JBang CLI now includes a complete platform management subsystem with several new commands (dbz#2176):

pipeline signal

Send signals to running pipelines (e.g., stop snapshot, force re-read).

source verify-signals

Verify that signaling is correctly configured for a source.

config set/get

Manage CLI settings such as the platform URL.

switch

Switch between multiple platform environments (development, staging, production) without passing connection details on every command.

Pipeline failure visibility

The Debezium Platform UI now displays pipeline deployment failures with their error details directly in the interface. Users can see what went wrong when a pipeline fails to deploy and trigger a re-deployment from the UI, eliminating the need to check server logs for troubleshooting. (dbz#2261)

Optional OIDC bearer token authentication

The Debezium Platform conductor now supports optional OIDC bearer token authentication for its API endpoints. When configured, all /api/* endpoints require a valid bearer token, while health check endpoints (/q/*) remain open.

This enables integration with identity providers like Keycloak for securing Platform API access in production environments. (dbz#2306)

Debezium Server

JDBC sink consumer delegates to the JDBC sink connector

Debezium Server now delegates all JDBC consumer operations to the JDBC sink connector, minimizing future maintenance and inheriting all future improvements to the sink connector out of the box. (dbz#2265)

Readiness probe for health checks

Debezium Server now includes a proper readiness health check that reflects whether the connector is actually ready to process changes. Previously, the /q/health/ready endpoint always returned UP as soon as the Quarkus application started, regardless of the connector’s actual state.

The new readiness probe checks the engine’s polling status, giving orchestration tools like Kubernetes an accurate signal for routing traffic. (dbz#2393)

Debezium for CockroachDB

Documentation and warnings for static capture sets

The CockroachDB connector now documents that table.include.list patterns are resolved once at startup, meaning tables created after the connector starts are not automatically captured. Additionally, an execute-snapshot signal targeting a table outside the running capture set now produces a clear warning instead of silently succeeding without emitting any rows. This aligns the CockroachDB connector’s behavior with all other Debezium connectors. (dbz#2392)

Debezium for Informix

Updated to Informix JDBC driver v15.0.1.4

The Informix connector now ships with the latest Informix JDBC driver version 15.0.1.4, bringing driver-level bug fixes and compatibility improvements. (dbz#2342)

TiDB Connector

Incubating TiDB connector

TiDB is an open-source, MySQL-compatible distributed SQL database designed for hybrid transactional and analytical processing (HTAP) workloads. It is commonly used in scenarios that require horizontal scalability, strong consistency, and high availability across large datasets.

An incubating Debezium connector for TiDB is now available, using Kafka-based change data capture. This enables users running TiDB to integrate with the broader Debezium ecosystem for real-time data streaming and event-driven architectures. (dbz#789)

Debezium AI for Python

Structured metadata filtering and reactive LangGraph agent

PyDebeziumAI now includes a unified metadata filtering API for vector store adapters, allowing consistent filter syntax across Chroma, PGVector, and Milvus backends. A new reactive LangGraph agent example demonstrates how CDC-driven updates can feed real-time context changes into AI agent decision-making. (dbz#2156)

Other fixes

  • Prevent potential PostgreSQL data loss on connector restart with in-progress transactions (dbz#51 dbz#76)

  • Fix multiple MySQL DDL parser errors (dbz#71 dbz#360 dbz#690 dbz#2321 dbz#2401)

  • Schema history no longer requires Kafka storage classes on the classpath (dbz#870)

  • Add Ansible-based host provisioning service for host deployment (dbz#2092)

  • Reuse RetryingRunnable for outbox consumer error handling (dbz#2136)

  • Fix IBMi TIMESTAMP tolerance regression introduced in 3.5.0.Beta2 (dbz#2153)

  • Add YashanDB integration tests and fix related code regressions (dbz#2205)

  • Fix incremental snapshots stopping after the database closes the connection (dbz#2275)

  • Fix startup failure with MongoDB and Db2 sources due to Quarkus bootstrap issue (dbz#2284)

  • Fix non-graceful Oracle OpenLogReplicator network client shutdown on interrupt (dbz#2299)

  • Fix Oracle blocking snapshot race condition when using OpenLogReplicator (dbz#2301)

  • Remove empty predicate from transform API responses (dbz#2308)

  • Fix Helm chart rendering duplicate role binding resources (dbz#2309)

  • Fix RabbitMQ sink ignoring routingKey.source=topic from environment variables (dbz#2317)

  • Fix retry delay strategy not being honored without auto-heal enabled (dbz#2329)

  • Fix PostgreSQL parallel snapshot producing inconsistent reads across pooled connections (dbz#2330)

  • Fix heartbeat.action.query causing NullPointerException for non-JDBC connectors (dbz#2339)

  • Fix Oracle LogMiner client ID exclusion filter not handling null values (dbz#2348)

  • Fix UNNEST batch writes failing on CockroachDB with binary columns (dbz#2357)

  • Upgrade Infinispan dependency to 16.2.2 for Oracle and Debezium Server (dbz#2365)

  • Fix Oracle LogMiner extended string parser failing on table aliases (dbz#2366)

  • Auto-generate conductor OpenAPI specification during build (dbz#2367)

entry.title: Debezium 3.6.1.Final Released
entry.content:
We’re pleased to announce the release of Debezium 3.6.1.Final, a maintenance release that delivers important data integrity and security improvements across multiple connectors.

This release fixes several issues that could affect change event accuracy, including correct parsing of BC-era dates in PostgreSQL, proper mapping of MySQL INTEGER UNSIGNED columns, and resolution of Oracle RowId corruption in change events. The JDBC sink connector also receives a fix for tsvector data handling, and credential leakage has been addressed in log output and configuration serialization.

Read on for the full details!

  • New features and improvements

  • Other changes

New Features and Improvements

The following covers all new features and improvements, grouped by connector component area.

Debezium Core

Debezium for MySQL

Debezium for Oracle

Debezium for PostgreSQL

Debezium JDBC sink

Debezium Storage

Debezium Core

Prevent credential leakage in configuration logging

When logging configuration properties, Debezium already masked database passwords but did not cover other sensitive values such as Azure Event Hubs connection strings containing shared access keys.

Configuration logging now masks all credential-bearing properties, preventing accidental exposure in log output. (dbz#27)

Debezium for MySQL

Consistent schema mapping for INTEGER UNSIGNED columns

Columns declared as INTEGER UNSIGNED (a synonym for INT UNSIGNED) were mapped to different schema types during snapshot versus streaming, which could cause schema mismatch errors in downstream consumers.

The connector now consistently maps INTEGER UNSIGNED to INT64 in both modes. (dbz#2172)

Debezium for Oracle

Fix for RowId corruption in change events

The internal encoding used to store Oracle ROWID values was silently truncating part of the identifier, causing the source.row_id field in change events to contain incorrect values for most tables.

The encoding now preserves the full ROWID, ensuring change events accurately reference the originating row. (dbz#2169)

Debezium for PostgreSQL

Correct parsing of BC-era dates

The PostgreSQL connector previously threw a DateTimeParseException when encountering BC-era date values such as 0002-11-30 00:00:00 BC or 0002-11-30 BC. The date parser now correctly handles the BC suffix, allowing these historical date values to be captured without errors. (dbz#1340)

Debezium JDBC sink

Correct tsvector handling for multi-word lexemes

When writing PostgreSQL tsvector values, the JDBC sink was stripping all single quotes from the data before binding. This silently corrupted any tsvector whose lexemes contain spaces or apostrophes — for example, 'new york' would be split into two separate tokens.

The connector now preserves the tsvector value as-is, ensuring lexeme boundaries and content remain intact. (dbz#2199)

Debezium Storage

Mask RocketMQ ACL secret key in configuration output

The RocketMQ storage configuration was rendering its ACL secret key in clear text whenever the configuration was logged or printed.

The secret key is now masked, consistent with how Debezium handles other sensitive values. (dbz#2188)

Other fixes

  • Event count reset for a transaction in progress (dbz#633)

  • Tombstones with JSONB column and table.expand.json.payload produce warning logs (dbz#1369)

  • Snapshot mode no_data incorrectly produces remaining tables JMX metric (dbz#1479)

  • PostgreSQL-to-PostgreSQL type preservation audit exposes several failures (dbz#2100)

  • Make internal.legacy.snapshot.max.threads option public (dbz#2150)

  • ZeroDateFallbackConverter truncates DATETIME(4-6) to millisecond precision (dbz#2187)

  • BIT columns dropped because VitessType does not resolve BIT (dbz#2191)

  • Incremental snapshot silently skipped if the underlying connection is re-opened (dbz#2204)

  • RocketMQ schema history recovery fails on large histories and aborts on corrupted records (dbz#2215)

  • Redis schema history silently drops all records after a corrupted entry during recovery (dbz#2221)

  • Duplicated type name BINARY BINARY emitted for BINARY columns (dbz#2223)

  • Predicates.excludesLiterals returns an includes predicate due to double negation (dbz#2246)

  • DdlNormalizer injects backticks into string literals and SQL comments matching reserved-keyword heuristics (dbz#2254)

  • Oracle secondary configuration should not require secondary.port (dbz#2257)

  • USING INDEX clause in ADD CONSTRAINT fails to parse (dbz#2272)

  • Archive log only mode advances SCN too early (dbz#2296)

In total, 27 issues were resolved in Debezium 3.6.1.Final. The list of changes can also be found in our release notes.

A big thank you to all the contributors from the community who worked diligently on this release:
