entry.title: Debezium 3.7.0.Alpha1 Released
entry.content:
As summer heats up, so does the pace of innovation in the Debezium community. We’re thrilled to announce Debezium 3.7.0.Alpha1, the first preview release of the 3.7 series, packed with new features and improvements.

Highlights include an incubating Ingres connector, a new ExtendedTimestamp type for high-precision timestamps, and expanded JDBC sink support with CockroachDB, SingleStore, and Starrocks dialects. The release also brings schema history memory optimization, Debezium Engine shutdown strategies, and numerous platform, connector, and performance improvements. Read on for the full details!

  • Breaking changes

  • New features and improvements

  • Other changes

Breaking changes

With any new release of software, there can be breaking changes. This release is no exception, so let’s discuss the major changes you should be aware of before upgrading to Debezium 3.7.0.Alpha1

Debezium JDBC sink

MySQL type preservation audit and fixes

Several MySQL data types that were previously silently corrupted or mishandled in MySQL-to-MySQL JDBC sink pipelines have been fixed. Users upgrading should verify their pipelines, as some behaviors that previously appeared to work (but produced wrong data) may now surface errors instead. Affected types include BIGINT UNSIGNED max values, BIT(>1) columns with Avro converters, ENUM/SET values containing commas or quotes, spatial coordinate ordering, and TIME values outside the standard clock range. (dbz#2102)

New Features and Improvements

The following covers all new features and improvements, grouped by connector component area.

Debezium Core

Debezium for Db2

Debezium for MySQL

Debezium for Oracle

Debezium for PostgreSQL

Debezium JDBC sink

Debezium Quarkus Extensions

Debezium Operator

Debezium Platform

Debezium Server

Debezium CLI

Debezium for CockroachDB

Debezium for Spanner

Debezium for YashanDB

Debezium for Ingres

Debezium Embedded Engine

PyDebeziumAI

Debezium Core

Schema history memory optimization

Deployments with many identically structured tables, such as multi-tenant databases where each tenant has its own schema, can now see significantly reduced memory consumption. Debezium now deduplicates schema history objects so that only one copy of each unique table, column, and attribute definition is retained in memory, rather than storing redundant copies for every structurally identical table. (dbz#1813)

Caching support for LOB re-selection

The ReselectColumnsPostProcessor can now cache re-selected column values, avoiding repeated database queries for large out-of-line columns (such as PostgreSQL TOAST columns or Oracle LOBs) that rarely change but sit on frequently-updated rows. When the same column value is needed across multiple events, it is served from the cache instead of querying the source database each time, significantly reducing load on the source.

The cache automatically invalidates entries when a real value change is detected, so correctness is maintained without relying on expiration alone. Caching is disabled by default and can be enabled with reselect.cache.enabled=true. (dbz#2002)

ExtendedTimestamp for high-precision timestamps beyond INT64 limits

Databases like PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server support timestamp ranges and precisions that can exceed what a single INT64 epoch value can represent, leading to silent overflow and data corruption for far-future dates or high-precision values.

A new io.debezium.time.ExtendedTimestamp semantic type addresses this by separating calendar range from sub-second precision, using a composite STRUCT with seconds and nanos fields. This approach follows the same design used by Java’s Instant and Google Protocol Buffers Timestamp, and eliminates the overflow risk that affected MicroTimestamp and NanoTimestamp at the boundaries of their representable ranges. (dbz#2119)

Debezium for Db2

Change table pruning support

Change tables captured by the DB2 Capture Agent can now be automatically pruned, preventing unbounded growth that previously required a separate Apply Agent to manage. After successfully producing change events, the connector signals the Capture Agent with the most recent processed position, allowing it to purge entries that are no longer needed. (dbz#1843)

Debezium for MySQL

CREATE TABLE …​ LIKE syntax support

The MySQL connector now correctly handles CREATE TABLE …​ LIKE DDL statements, which create a new table using the structure of an existing table. Previously, this common MySQL pattern could cause schema tracking issues, potentially leading to missed or incorrectly shaped change events for the newly created table. (dbz#248)

Debezium for Oracle

ROWID surrogate key sorting by primary key

Incremental snapshots using the ROWID pseudocolumn as a surrogate key can now execute significantly faster. Previously, the snapshot query sorted by ROWID, which can be very expensive on large tables. The connector now uses the table’s primary key for ordering while still projecting ROWID as the surrogate key, avoiding the costly sort without changing the snapshot behavior. (dbz#1726)

Downstream mining support

The Oracle connector now supports downstream mining for both XStream and LogMiner adapters. Downstream mining allows users to move all change data capture mining operations to a dedicated standby environment, where archive logs are replayed for analytics and CDC purposes. This avoids placing mining load on the production database and lets DBAs tune the downstream environment independently.

In this mode, all snapshot and metadata queries are routed to the primary database, while change capture operations occur on the downstream system. (dbz#1868)

Debezium for PostgreSQL

First-class geometric type mapping

Tables containing PostgreSQL geometric columns (box, circle, line, lseg, path, polygon) now produce usable, structured change events instead of opaque binary data. Previously, these types had no explicit mapping, so their values were either dropped entirely or emitted as raw bytes that downstream consumers couldn’t interpret.

The types box, lseg, path, and polygon are mapped to the existing Geometry Struct using WKB encoding, with an extension field that preserves the original PostgreSQL type. The circle and line types receive new dedicated Struct schemas (io.debezium.data.geometry.Circle and io.debezium.data.geometry.Line) because they have no faithful Well-Known Binary representation. (dbz#2135)

Debezium JDBC sink

Starrocks catalog name support

Users connecting to a Starrocks target through the MySQL driver can now specify the desired catalog name with a new dialect.starrocks.catalog_name option. Previously, the driver defaulted to a schema that did not match the intended catalog, with no way to override it. (dbz#979)

JMX metrics support

The JDBC sink connector now exposes JMX metrics, giving users visibility into what is actually happening at the target database. These complement the standard Kafka Connect sink task metrics by describing operations beyond the connector’s put() boundary. (dbz#1174)

Metric Name Description

TotalNumberOfWrites

Total number of processed events (insert/update/upsert) applied to the target database.

TotalNumberOfDeletes

Total number of delete operations applied to the target database.

TotalNumberOfTruncates

Total number of truncate operations applied to the target database.

TotalNumberOfFilteredEvents

Number of records skipped without being applied, such as unresolvable tables, disabled deletes/truncates, or schema-change events.

TotalNumberOfTablesCreated

Total number of tables the sink created in the target database when schema evolution is enabled.

TotalNumberOfTablesAltered

Total number of tables the sink altered in the target database when schema evolution is enabled.

CockroachDB dialect support

CockroachDB users can now use Hibernate’s native CockroachDialect with the JDBC sink without losing upsert support. Previously, the sink did not recognize this dialect and fell back to a generic mode that could not generate INSERT …​ ON CONFLICT …​ DO UPDATE statements, forcing users to manually override with PostgreSQLDialect as a workaround. A dedicated CockroachDB dialect provider now handles this automatically. (dbz#1639)

SingleStore database support

The JDBC sink connector can now write directly to SingleStore, a distributed SQL database that is compatible with the MySQL wire protocol but has its own SQL syntax and type-handling differences. A dedicated dialect ensures correct DML operations without requiring manual configuration workarounds. Geospatial type support is planned for a future release. (dbz#2146)

Startup validation with validate-only schema evolution mode

A new schema.evolution=validate-only mode catches missing target tables at startup rather than waiting for the first record to arrive. For low-traffic topics, this can mean the difference between discovering a configuration problem in seconds versus hours.

This mode is designed for deployments where target tables are managed externally (e.g., by a DDL pipeline) and the connector should only perform DML. It validates statically resolvable table names using the default collection naming strategy; configurations that rely on ${source.*} placeholders in the collection name format or custom naming strategies are not eligible for startup validation. When topics.regex is used, validation is deferred until topic assignment. (dbz#2179)

Debezium Quarkus Extensions

Debezium Server configuration convention support

Users can now configure the Quarkus extension using Debezium Server’s canonical debezium. configuration prefix, in addition to the existing quarkus.debezium. prefix. This alignment simplifies configuration when moving between the two systems, and is part of the broader effort to enable native execution support for Debezium Server. (dbz#1690)

Debezium Operator

Conductor and operator level metrics

The Debezium Platform now exposes conductor and operator level metrics through the JMX Exporter, providing visibility into memory, CPU consumption, and other operational metrics beyond the existing pipeline-level metrics. This gives operators a more complete picture of the platform’s resource utilization and health. (dbz#1918)

Debezium Platform

Integrated documentation access

The Debezium Platform UI now provides quick access to relevant documentation directly within the interface, allowing users to reference connector configuration and operational guidance without leaving the platform. (dbz#1570)

Boolean and integer value types in configuration UI

The Debezium Platform UI now supports entering boolean and integer value types for additional configuration properties in source and destination configurations. Previously, only free-style text input was available for properties not part of the standard configuration schema, limiting the ability to correctly specify non-string values. (dbz#1859)

Reduced OTel metrics latency

Monitoring metrics in the Debezium Platform now appear much faster, with worst-case latency reduced from approximately 90 seconds to 26 seconds. Previously, conservative defaults for OpenTelemetry scrape and export intervals meant that short-lived snapshots could complete before their metrics ever appeared. The platform now automatically configures more responsive defaults when OTel is enabled, making real-time observation of snapshot progress and event throughput practical. (dbz#2168)

Glass contrast mode

The Debezium Platform Stage UI now supports a Glass contrast mode toggle, allowing users to switch between the default and glass contrast themes. In dark theme, glass contrast is preferred by default for enhanced visibility. User preferences are stored across sessions, following the PatternFly glass mode design guidelines. (dbz#2212)

Debezium Server

Smarter sink-to-storage property remapping

When the sink and storage backends use the same technology (e.g., Redis) but with different endpoints, Debezium Server could previously overwrite explicitly configured storage properties with sink properties, leading to subtle misconfiguration.

The automatic sink-to-storage property remapping now respects explicit storage configuration; if schema.history.internal or offset.storage sub-properties are already set, the remapping is skipped. The original convenience behavior, where sink properties are shared with storage when no explicit storage configuration exists, continues to work as before. (dbz#2078)

Native distribution module for Debezium Server

Debezium Server can now be built as a native executable, enabling faster startup times and lower memory footprint compared to the traditional JVM distribution. A new debezium-server-native-dist module provides the build configuration and packaging needed for native compilation. (dbz#2108)

Debezium CLI

Connection and transform management commands

The Debezium JBang CLI has been extended with new commands for managing connections and transforms in the Debezium Platform. Users can now list, get, create, update, delete, and validate connections, as well as list available schemas and collections. Transform commands provide full CRUD operations for managing data transformations. (dbz#2077)

Pipeline log access and catalog discovery commands

The Debezium JBang CLI now includes commands for accessing pipeline logs and discovering available connector catalogs. The debezium pipeline logs command supports both full log dump download and live tail streaming over WebSocket, providing a kubectl logs -f equivalent for Debezium pipelines. Catalog commands let users list available connector descriptors and inspect specific component configurations for the current platform version. (dbz#2143)

Debezium for CockroachDB

Configurable changefeed strategy

Users can now choose how changefeeds are created with a new cockroachdb.changefeed.strategy option. The single strategy (default) creates one multi-table changefeed, which CockroachDB recommends for clusters with many tables. The per-table strategy creates a separate changefeed per table, providing better parallelism, fault isolation, and the ability to tune settings like resolved intervals independently for each table. (dbz#1636)

Sinkless changefeed support

The CockroachDB connector can now stream change events directly over the SQL connection using sinkless (core) changefeeds, eliminating the need for an intermediate Kafka cluster. Previously, the connector required CockroachDB to push changes to a separate Kafka cluster first, which meant managing a second Kafka client and its associated configuration.

With sinkless changefeeds, the connector produces directly to the output topics like other Debezium connectors, inheriting the worker’s existing Kafka configuration automatically. (dbz#2024)

Debezium for Spanner

Placement tables support

The Spanner change stream connector now supports placement tables, expanding the scope of tables that can be monitored for change data capture. (dbz#1415)

Debezium for YashanDB

Incubating YashanDB connector

Debezium now includes an incubating connector for YashanDB, a high-performance enterprise database system developed by the Shenzhen Institute of Computing Sciences (SICS). YashanDB supports stand-alone, shared-cluster, and distributed deployments, covering OLTP, HTAP, and OLAP workloads, and is widely adopted in industries such as finance, government, telecommunications, and energy. It also offers a high degree of Oracle compatibility, making it a common choice in environments that are migrating away from Oracle.

With this new connector, Debezium extends its change data capture reach to YashanDB deployments, enabling real-time data integration for organizations that rely on it as part of their data infrastructure. (dbz#1680)

Debezium for Ingres

Incubating Ingres connector

Debezium now includes an incubating connector for Actian Ingres, one of the earliest relational database systems, with roots tracing back to a UC Berkeley research project in the 1970s. Today, Ingres is an ultra-reliable enterprise transactional database used by thousands of organizations worldwide across industries such as aviation, government, and financial services. It supports both row-based and columnar storage, MVCC, and hybrid OLTP/analytic workloads.

With this new connector, Debezium brings change data capture to Ingres deployments, enabling real-time streaming of data changes into downstream systems for organizations looking to modernize their data integration pipelines. (dbz#1462)

Debezium Embedded Engine

Shutdown strategies

Applications embedding the Debezium Engine can now define custom conditions for gracefully stopping the engine, such as shutting down after a snapshot completes, after processing a fixed number of events, or when the event queue has been fully drained. Previously, there was no built-in way to stop the engine based on runtime conditions, requiring applications to implement their own external shutdown logic. (dbz#1745)

PyDebeziumAI

Synchronization layer and Chroma vector store integration

PyDebeziumAI now supports end-to-end real-time synchronization between CDC event streams and a Chroma vector database. A new synchronization layer automatically translates database changes into the appropriate vector store operations, keeping vector embeddings in sync as source data is inserted, updated, or deleted. (dbz#2040)

PGVector and Milvus backend support

Users can now choose from multiple vector database backends, with new PGVector and Milvus adapters joining the existing ChromaDB support. This release also introduces standardized logging and observability across all PyDebeziumAI modules, making it easier to monitor and troubleshoot the CDC-to-vector synchronization pipeline. (dbz#2128)

Other fixes

  • Avoid logging Azure Event Hub connection string (dbz#27)

  • Order field definitions in config classes according to field group and position (dbz#453)

  • Error caused by database name containing SQL keywords (dbz#1176)

  • Remove empty facets from OpenLineage events (dbz#1234)

  • The poll.interval.ms connector property is capped at 5 seconds by ChangeEventQueue (dbz#1644)

  • Move TOPIC_PREFIX configuration from CONNECTION group to CONNECTOR group (dbz#1821)

  • Incremental snapshot is abandoned if the emit window open query fails with a recoverable exception (dbz#2105)

  • Chunked snapshot fails with SQL syntax error for tables whose names require quoting (dbz#2173)

  • RocketMqSchemaHistory does not shut down its MQ producer on stop, leaking resources (dbz#2196)

  • ANTLR parser fails on ALTER ADD COLUMN with ALGORITHM=INSTANT (dbz#1439)

  • ZeroDateFallbackConverter truncates DATETIME(4-6) to millisecond precision (dbz#2187)

  • MongoDB connector does not retry connection on initial failure (dbz#67)

  • Cannot compare binlog filenames with different base names (dbz#75)

  • Snapshot mode no_data incorrectly produces remaining tables JMX metric (dbz#1479)

  • INTEGER UNSIGNED synonym maps to INT32 instead of INT64, diverging from snapshot (dbz#2172)

  • OSON values not parsed correctly due to missing JSON prefix in HEXTORAW detection (dbz#1884)

  • Make internal.legacy.snapshot.max.threads option public as legacy.snapshot.max.threads (dbz#2150)

  • RowIdCodec silently discards high bits, producing corrupted row_id values (dbz#2169)

  • PostgreSQL TypeRegistry emits spurious type already mapped warnings (dbz#1323)

  • DateTimeParseException for BC-era date values (dbz#1340)

  • Tombstones with JSONB column and expanded JSON payload produce spurious warnings (dbz#1369)

  • Connector fails to start due to type registry collisions with Oracle compatibility types (dbz#1400)

  • PostgreSQL source with JDBC copy mode can lose data (dbz#1554)

  • Document that re-creating replication slots after failover is unnecessary with PostgreSQL 17 failover slots (dbz#2095)

  • Add reflection instrumentation for ConfigInfos and ConfigInfo (dbz#2170)

  • Make configuration map mutable for AgroalDatasourceConfiguration (dbz#2171)

  • Debezium Operator system tests fail (dbz#2181)

  • Update UI to use connector catalog API for sources and destinations (dbz#1207)

  • Add description field to connections API payload (dbz#1245)

  • Duplicate key violations should be more visible to users (dbz#1427)

  • Add deployment mode selection with CDI wiring (dbz#2087)

  • Cannot immediately create a new connection after deleting one (dbz#2115)

  • Provide feedback when pipeline deployment fails due to skipped outbox event (dbz#2125)

  • Add ability to refresh list panels in pipeline monitoring (dbz#2164)

entry.title: Running the Debezium Platform on AWS: PostgreSQL to Amazon Kinesis

link.title: Running the Debezium Platform on AWS: PostgreSQL to Amazon Kinesis

entry.content:
In his recent mid-year update, Mario highlighted the incredible work he and his team have done to make the Debezium Platform operational on Kubernetes. So let us take it somewhere concrete: Amazon Web Services.

This post stands the Platform up on a single-node k3s cluster on an EC2 instance and builds a real change-data-capture pipeline from Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL to Amazon Kinesis. The deployment itself is done through a couple of simple commands via a companion project that does the heavy lifting, so the focus is the AWS-specific friction that documentation is thin on: IAM for the Kinesis sink, Kinesis stream naming, RDS logical replication, and reading a change event back out of the stream to prove it all works.

  • The setup: the Platform on k3s on EC2

  • The source: PostgreSQL on RDS

  • The destination: an IAM-first Kinesis sink

  • Building and running the pipeline

  • The proof: a change event out of Kinesis

  • Wrapping up

The setup: the Platform on any VM, in a handful of commands

The Platform runs on Kubernetes, and k3s is a good fit for a single cloud box: one binary, a built-in Traefik ingress controller, and a local-path storage provisioner — everything the Platform’s Helm releases expect, without the weight of a full cluster.

You do not have to wire that up by hand. A companion project, debezium-platform-lab, automates the whole deployment with mage targets orchestrating helmfile releases. mage is a task runner whose targets are plain Go functions; each one here invokes helmfile, which installs an entire set of Helm releases — their versions, values, and dependency order — from one declarative file, collapsing a multi-chart deployment into a single command. It targets any VM you can reach over SSH — an EC2 instance here, but equally a bare-metal box or a VM on your desk.

Clone it, copy the example environment file, and set a handful of variables:

git clone https://github.com/pxcamus/debezium-platform-lab
cd debezium-platform-lab
cp .env.example .env

The variables that matter for a remote VM:

DBZ_VERSION=3.6.0          # Debezium Platform Helm chart version
CLUSTER_TYPE=k3s           # provision k3s on a remote host over SSH
DBZ_ENV=aws                # selects deploy/values/<component>/aws.yaml
DBZ_DOMAIN=aws.example.io  # base DNS zone; the UI is served at dmp.<DBZ_DOMAIN>

K3S_HOST=<vm-ip-or-ssh-alias>
K3S_SSH_USER=ec2-user      # ubuntu, admin, ... depending on the AMI
K3S_SSH_KEY=~/.ssh/your-key.pem
K3S_LOCAL_KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config_aws  # where cluster:recreate writes the kubeconfig

Running it locally instead? Set CLUSTER_TYPE=kind and DBZ_ENV=local, and the same mage targets deploy the Platform onto a local Kind cluster — no VM required. The tooling is the same; only the two environment variables change.

Then two phases. First, provision the cluster — it will SSH into the VM, installs k3s, and pulls back a kubeconfig pointed at the box:

mage cluster:recreate

Second, deploy the stack, ordered by dependency — the OpenTelemetry-based monitoring, the Debezium Operator, and the Platform itself:

mage helm:monitoring     # kube-prometheus-stack + OpenTelemetry operator
mage helm:platform       # Conductor + Stage (the Platform UI)

That is the whole deployment. mage -l lists every target, and mage helm:all brings up the batteries-included CDC stack (Kafka, in-cluster databases, and all) if you want it — that fuller stack and its local-path volumes need more disk than a default EBS root, so size the instance accordingly (40 GB was comfortable here).

Beyond the deploy, you have full cluster access: mage cluster:recreate already fetched a kubeconfig pointed at the box — the mage helm:* targets use it automatically, and you can too. Point kubectl or k9s at it, and you are connected to your cluster :

KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config_aws k9s

The UI and Grafana are reached by hostname through Traefik, so in a demo without real DNS you need those names to resolve to the instance. Point them at the EC2 public IP in your /etc/hosts:

<ec2-public-ip>  dmp.aws.example.io grafana.aws.example.io

In all, the demo needs just three inbound ports open to your IP — 22 for SSH (used by mage to initially create the cluster), 6443 for kubectl and k9s, and 80 for the Platform UI — with nothing exposed to the wider internet:

The Source in that screenshot (79.116.219.5/32) is my own workstation’s IP — use yours.

A completed deploy leaves you with two things to look at. The Platform’s UI, served through Traefik at dmp.<DBZ_DOMAIN>:

And a Grafana instance from the bundled kube-prometheus-stack, for cluster-level metrics — distinct from the Platform’s own pipeline dashboard we will use later:

Two AWS-flavoured adjustments the aws values handle for you: there is no cert-manager, so the OpenTelemetry operator’s admission webhook uses a self-signed certificate and the UI is served over plain HTTP through Traefik. And because pods reach AWS services over the VPC’s private network, the connector talks to RDS privately, never over the public internet.

The Platform’s integrated monitoring — the OpenTelemetry-based dashboard Mario described — works unchanged on AWS. Once the pipeline is running you get event throughput, replication lag, queue utilisation, and snapshot progress out of the box, which is exactly how we will confirm the pipeline later.

With the Platform reachable, the interesting work begins: the two ends of the pipeline.

The source: PostgreSQL on RDS

PostgreSQL is not the point of this post — the Platform is — and the connector is already thoroughly documented, so we keep the source deliberately light. For the demo we ran a db.t4g.micro instance: cheap, Free-Tier-eligible, and plenty for a handful of tables.

Just one thing is genuinely RDS-specific. Logical replication is not a postgresql.conf edit, and the default parameter group is read-only, so create a custom one (Aurora and RDS → Parameter groups → Create, family postgres18), set rds.logical_replication = 1, assign it to the instance (Databases → your instance → Modify), and reboot — the parameter is static. Confirm with SHOW wal_level; — you want logical.

Everything else is two small scripts, run through the SSH tunnel to the private instance — a local port-forward via the k3s box — as the RDS master user. Both live in the companion example in the debezium-examples repository.

setup.sql takes the good-practice path rather than the quickest one: it does not reuse the admin user for change data capture. It creates an app_owner that owns the ecommerce database and its schema — standing in for a real application — a dedicated, read-only debezium user for capture, the tables, and a little seed data. Two lines in it are the RDS catch worth knowing: replication is granted through the managed rds_replication role (WITH REPLICATION is superuser-only on RDS), and the publication is created up front by the table owner — the non-superuser debezium user cannot autocreate it, which otherwise leaves you with a replication slot but no publication.

ssh -N -L 5432:<rds-endpoint>:5432 dmp-demo                          # terminal 1
psql -h localhost -p 5432 -U <master-user> -d postgres -f setup.sql  # terminal 2

generate_products.sql tops up the products table with synthetic rows through the same tunnel — a simple, painless way to generate change events once the pipeline is live:

psql -h localhost -p 5432 -U <master-user> -d ecommerce -f generate_products.sql

The handful of settings the connector then needs — plugin (pgoutput), slot, publication (dbz_ecommerce), and auto-create mode (disabled, since setup.sql already created it) — are set right in the Platform’s configuration UI, under Connection Advanced Replication, with no digging through documentation for property names:

The Platform validates the connection on save; a green result means it can reach RDS, authenticate, and use the slot and publication. The source is real.

The destination: an IAM-first Kinesis sink

Creating a Kinesis stream is trivial; on-demand mode avoids shard-capacity planning:

aws kinesis create-stream --stream-name aws-demo.public.products \
  --stream-mode-details StreamMode=ON_DEMAND --region eu-south-2

Two things about a Kinesis sink are less obvious.

Stream names must match topic names. The Debezium Server Kinesis sink writes each change event to a stream named after the event’s topic, which for a PostgreSQL source is <topic-prefix>.<schema>.<table>. So capturing three tables means three streams — aws-demo.public.products, aws-demo.public.orders, and so on — each named after its topic. A single stream named after the prefix alone receives nothing, and events fail with ResourceNotFoundException.

Credentials belong on the instance, not in the cluster. This is the part worth doing carefully. The sink authenticates through the AWS SDK’s default credential chain. On a plain EC2 k3s cluster there is no IRSA, so the right answer is an IAM role attached to the EC2 instance: the SDK pulls temporary, auto-rotated credentials from the instance metadata service, and no static keys ever touch Kubernetes. Give that role a least-privilege policy scoped to your stream ARNs:

{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": ["kinesis:PutRecord", "kinesis:PutRecords", "kinesis:DescribeStream"],
  "Resource": "arn:aws:kinesis:eu-south-2:<account-id>:stream/aws-demo.public.*"
}

Create the role under IAM → Roles → Create role, choosing AWS service → EC2 as the trusted entity and attaching the policy above; AWS creates a matching instance profile for you. Then bind it to the box under EC2 → Instances → select your instance → Actions → Security → Modify IAM role.

With that identity living on the instance, the Platform’s Kinesis destination connection needs almost nothing. The sink resolves its credentials from the instance role at runtime, so the connection form has a single configuration property — the region:

That near-empty form is the payoff of doing the IAM properly: the sensitive part — who is allowed to write to the stream — lives in a role attached to the instance, not as an access key pasted into, and then stored by, the Platform.

Building and running the pipeline

With both ends ready, the pipeline is a source, an optional transform, and a destination:

The transform stays empty here on purpose. Because we created one Kinesis stream per table, the topic names Debezium emits already match real stream names. If you preferred a single shared stream, this is where io.debezium.transforms.ByLogicalTableRouter would collapse every topic onto one name: topic.regex matches the topics to re-route, topic.replacement names the single destination they all land on.

Worth noting what is not in that picture. Single message transforms are a Kafka Connect concept, and every SMT in the Platform’s picker carries a Kafka Connect class name — but there is no Kafka and no Kafka Connect anywhere in this deployment. The Platform runs connectors on the Debezium engine, which applies the same transforms chain in-process before handing each record to the sink.

Start the pipeline, and the Platform’s monitoring dashboard confirms it end to end — connection status, snapshot progress, and replication lag, all without setting up your own observability stack:

Connected, snapshot Completed, sub-millisecond source lag, zero errors. But a healthy dashboard only proves the source side is happy. To prove data reached Kinesis, read it back.

The proof: a change event out of Kinesis

Pull the oldest record straight from the shard and decode it:

SHARD=$(aws kinesis get-shard-iterator --stream-name aws-demo.public.products \
  --shard-id shardId-000000000000 --shard-iterator-type TRIM_HORIZON \
  --region eu-south-2 --query ShardIterator --output text)

aws kinesis get-records --shard-iterator "$SHARD" --region eu-south-2 \
  --query 'Records[0].Data' --output text | base64 --decode | jq .payload

Out comes a familiar Debezium envelope:

{
  "before": null,
  "after": {
    "id": "prod-005",
    "name": "Designing Data-Intensive Applications",
    "price": "FXw=",
    "stock_quantity": 60
  },
  "source": { "connector": "postgresql", "db": "ecommerce", "table": "products",
              "snapshot": "true", "lsn": 1543504240 },
  "op": "r"
}

op: "r" is a read — a row seen during the initial snapshot. A live UPDATE arrives as op: "u" with before and after populated, an insert as "c", a delete as "d". It is the same envelope Debezium produces everywhere; the only AWS-specific detail is that it arrived as a base64-encoded Kinesis Data blob.

Which brings us to the one field that makes everyone think something is broken: "price": "FXw=".

That is not corruption. PostgreSQL NUMERIC/DECIMAL columns are serialised by default with decimal.handling.mode = precise: the unscaled integer in two’s-complement bytes, base64-encoded, with the scale carried in the schema. Decode it and it resolves:

$ printf 'FXw=' | base64 -d | xxd
00000000: 157c                                     .|
# 0x157C = 5500, scale 2  ->  55.00

55.00 — exact and lossless, but not human-readable. If your consumers would rather have a plain value, set decimal.handling.mode to string ("55.00", no precision loss) or double (readable, but floating point — not for currency).

The Debezium documentation covers this thoroughly.

Wrapping up

That is a complete, observable PostgreSQL-to-Kinesis CDC pipeline on AWS: change events leaving RDS, crossing a least-privilege IAM boundary, and landing in a Kinesis stream you can read. The same pipeline shape extends naturally to other cloud sources. A follow-up post will swap PostgreSQL for Amazon DocumentDB, where the one new variable is TLS: the connector must trust DocumentDB’s certificate authority, which means mounting a truststore into the deployment — exactly what recent Platform Helm chart work enables.

Hopefully this post helps you enjoy the amazing work the Debezium team has done to greatly reduce the operational workload of running a CDC pipeline.
entry.summary: In his recent mid-year update, Mario highlighted the incredible work he and his team have done to make the Debezium Platform operational on Kubernetes. So let us take it somewhere concrete: Amazon Web Services. This post stands the Platform up on a single-node k3s cluster on an EC2 instance and builds a real change-data-capture pipeline from Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL to Amazon Kinesis. The deployment itself is done through a couple of simple commands via a companion project that does the heavy lifting, so the focus is the AWS-specific friction that documentation is thin on: IAM for the Kinesis sink, Kinesis stream naming, RDS logical replication, and reading a change event back out of the stream to prove it all works.

entry.title: Debezium Platform: Mid-Year Update (2026)
entry.content:
Hello Debezium community, Mario here. I have been leading the development of the Debezium Platform for nearly two years now, and it has been about a year since my last update on the project. I took a moment to reflect on what we have worked on recently, what we intend to work on by the end of the year, and the current status of the Debezium Platform.

A lot of work was done in the last year, but I don’t want to mimic a release note, even though I greatly value small fixes and features. Instead, I would like to highlight what I think, in my opinion, is really worth mentioning.

What’s new

Enhanced configuration UI

As you know, Debezium has a lot of configurations that give the flexibility to adapt and fine-tune it to different users' needs. Some configurations are cross-connector, while others are connector-specific, and others are just related to a very specific functionality. Debezium users, including those working with both Kafka Connect connectors and the server, are accustomed to working with text-based configuration files. So they discover the configurations and their meaning in the documentation, and that’s fine.

The idea behind the Debezium Platform was, and still is, to offer users a simplified way to define data pipelines, with a focus on design. From the beginning, we were clear that users should be able to configure each piece of the pipeline through a clear interface that presents all available options, indicates which settings are required, provides sensible default values where applicable, and supports conditional configuration based on other selected options. Nothing special, just something that any user would expect in a user interface.

We worked on this in the first part of the year, so we moved from the following UX.

to this

This is not intended to be a technical post, but I have to say it was not simple, as it affected multiple Debezium components. If you are curious about the details, you can have a look at DDD-13: Debezium Component Descriptors.

There are still some things to improve. For example, configuration grouping and order are not perfect, but at least there is now a basis for improving them.

Integrated monitoring

One of the most commonly requested features for the day 2 activities was observability. Debezium largely adopted JMX as the way to expose metrics in the connector and server, leaving end users with the observability stack setup and configuration. With the Platform, we wanted to simplify setup as much as possible by providing an integrated dashboard to monitor your pipelines. You can track key metrics such as event throughput, replication lag, queue utilization, snapshot progress, etc.

This is what the monitoring dashboard looks like

We opted for the OpenTelemetry standard, collecting metrics from Debezium Server with OpenTelemetry Java Agent via OpenTelemetry Collector. For those interested in the details, you can take a look at DDD-38: Pipeline Monitoring for Debezium Platform and documentation.

Bonus: AI experiments

At the end of last year, we designed a POC to integrate an AI chatbot into the Platform, with the idea of letting users interact with it in a conversational way. We got some good results, but the status is not yet at a point where we want to release it. We plan to continue working on it throughout the year. So keep an eye on it.

What’s next

Alerting

Having a monitoring dashboard is good, but having a way to be proactively alerted when things start to go wrong is much better. This is why we want to offer the possibility to configure alerts to be notified when a certain metric reaches a defined threshold.

Identity Access Management

One of the biggest limitations of the Platform today is its assumption of a trusted environment. This is perfectly fine when you are evaluating it locally or running it in a small team, but it quickly becomes an issue when multiple users and teams need to share the same instance.

This is why Identity and Access Management is one of the next major areas we want to tackle.

The goal is not just to add a login page. We want to provide proper authentication and authorization so that administrators can control who can access the Platform and what they are allowed to do. For example, some users may only need to monitor pipelines, while others should be able to create, modify, or delete them. Likewise, in a shared environment, different teams should be able to manage only their own pipelines, without seeing or accidentally modifying pipelines owned by other teams, while administrators retain full visibility across the entire Platform.

This will also lay the foundation for future enterprise-oriented features, making the Platform better suited to shared environments and production deployments.

We are still defining the details, but the current direction is to integrate with standard identity providers, allowing organizations to leverage their existing authentication infrastructure instead of managing users separately.

Host-based deployment

There was a recurring request from the community for a Debezium Server UI, even though we are offering the Debezium Platform. The reason is that Debezium Platform, though it was designed to deploy pipelines across different environments, only supports Kubernetes as of now. This is going to change.

Divyanshu Kumar, a Google Summer Of Code contributor, is working on DDD-41: Host-Based Pipeline Deployment for the Debezium Platform.

With his work, the Platform will provision your bare-metal machines via Ansible, preparing them to run your pipelines.

This is not a user interface served directly by Debezium Server; it’s much more. You can manage multiple Debezium Server instances (pipelines) from the same dashboard. DBZ-2085 tracks the feature progress.

Conclusion

I hope this helped you to have an overview of the current Platform status and where we would like to go. We remain steadfast in making the Platform a complete solution that enables the community to easily use the entire Debezium ecosystem of components.

If you like the project, you can help with your feedback, reporting issues, and, if you like, share your appreciation with a star.

That’s all I have for now. I’ll try to provide a twice-yearly update. So let’s touch base at the end of the year.

entry.title: Building Kafka-Less Data Integration Pipelines with Debezium

link.title: Building Kafka-Less Data Integration Pipelines with Debezium

entry.content:
Debezium is often associated with Kafka, and while this was true in the project’s early days, it is no longer the case. We explained in detail, together with several other common misconceptions, in our recent article, "What Nobody Explains About Debezium in 2026 (But Should)".

In this article, we’ll build on that discussion by showing the recently added JDBC sink support in Debezium Server (DS) and the Debezium Management Platform (DMP), which opens up Kafka-less data replication and migration scenarios.

Data integration, whether for one-shot migrations or continuous replication between databases, is one of the core use cases Debezium supports. Debezium has always focused on the CDC side of the problem: capturing changes from a database and turning them into a stream of change events. In the past, users had to develop their own consumer to write those events into a target database. To address this, we introduced the JDBC Sink Connector in the 2.2.0.Beta1 release in 2023, enabling end-to-end replication out of the box. The primary goal was not just to provide another database sink, but to provide full end-to-end support for Debezium’s native change event format, including source metadata and change semantics, without requiring event transformation or loss of context. At the time, this level of support for Debezium’s native events was not available in traditional relational database consumers.

Today, the same capability is available through the DS JDBC sink and within the DMP. This is not intended to replace Kafka Connect (KC) connectors. Instead, it provides an alternative for the users who do not have a KC cluster, or who do not need the scalability and high availability that KC offers, and simply want to move data between two databases. In those cases, DS or DMP can now be an attractive option, and with the upcoming native build support, DS will be able to run as a single native executable with minimal resource footprint.

All the examples shown in this article are available in the debezium-examples repository.

Data Integration with Debezium Server

Let’s see how simple it is to run a data migration pipeline with a few commands.

The requirement is to have the source and the destination database up and running, so we can easily start them up with the following Docker Compose file:

infrastructure-compose.yaml
services:
  postgres:
    container_name: postgres
    image: quay.io/debezium/example-postgres:3.6
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    environment:
      - POSTGRES_USER=postgres
      - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres
    networks:
      - backend

  mysql:
    container_name: mysql
    image: mysql:9.1
    ports:
      - "3306:3306"
    environment:
      - MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=debezium
      - MYSQL_DATABASE=target_db
    networks:
      - backend

networks:
  backend:
    name: debezium-jdbc-backend

running the Docker Compose command below:

docker compose -f infrastructure-compose.yaml up -d

Once you have this, you can start replicating your data with the following command:

 docker run --name inventory-pipeline -d \
    -v $(pwd)/application.properties:/debezium/config/application.properties:z \
    -p 8080:8080 \
    --network debezium-jdbc-backend \
    quay.io/debezium/server:nightly

The configuration used is the following

application.properties
debezium.sink.type=jdbc
debezium.sink.jdbc.connection.url=jdbc:mysql://mysql:3306/target_db
debezium.sink.jdbc.connection.username=root
debezium.sink.jdbc.connection.password=debezium
debezium.sink.jdbc.insert.mode=upsert
debezium.sink.jdbc.primary.key.mode=record_key
debezium.sink.jdbc.schema.evolution=basic
debezium.sink.jdbc.delete.enabled=true
debezium.source.connector.class=io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector
debezium.source.offset.storage.file.filename=data/offsets.dat
debezium.source.offset.flush.interval.ms=0
debezium.source.database.hostname=postgres
debezium.source.database.port=5432
debezium.source.database.user=postgres
debezium.source.database.password=postgres
debezium.source.database.dbname=postgres
debezium.source.topic.prefix=migration
debezium.source.schema.include.list=inventory
quarkus.log.console.json=false

While most of the configuration is standard Debezium source connector setup, a few properties are worth highlighting because they define how changes are applied to the target database.

The sink is configured to use the JDBC connector (debezium.sink.type=jdbc) and write changes to the MySQL instance specified by debezium.sink.jdbc.connection.url. The insert.mode=upsert setting instructs the connector to either insert new rows or update existing ones when a matching primary key is found. To determine the primary key, the connector uses the event key (primary.key.mode=record_key), which is derived from the source table’s primary key.

Another important setting is schema.evolution=basic, which enables the connector to automatically create or evolve destination tables as the source schema changes. Finally, delete.enabled=true ensures that delete operations captured from PostgreSQL are propagated to MySQL, keeping both databases synchronized.

The remaining properties configure the PostgreSQL source connector, specifying the database connection details and restricting change capture to the inventory schema.

Now, let’s check that the data has been correctly migrated to the MySQL database.

docker exec -it mysql mysql -uroot -pdebezium target_db -e "SELECT * FROM migration_inventory_customers;"
docker exec -it mysql mysql -uroot -pdebezium target_db -e "SELECT * FROM migration_inventory_products;"
docker exec -it mysql mysql -uroot -pdebezium target_db -e "SELECT * FROM migration_inventory_orders;"
docker exec -it mysql mysql -uroot -pdebezium target_db -e "SELECT * FROM migration_inventory_products_on_hand;"

You should see something like the following

+------+------------+-----------+-----------------------+
| id   | first_name | last_name | email                 |
+------+------------+-----------+-----------------------+
| 1001 | Sally      | Thomas    | sally.thomas@acme.com |
| 1002 | George     | Bailey    | gbailey@foobar.com    |
| 1003 | Edward     | Walker    | ed@walker.com         |
| 1004 | Anne       | Kretchmar | annek@noanswer.org    |

| id  | name               | description                                             | weight |
+-----+--------------------+---------------------------------------------------------+--------+
| 101 | scooter            | Small 2-wheel scooter                                   |   3.14 |
| 102 | car battery        | 12V car battery                                         |    8.1 |
| 103 | 12-pack drill bits | 12-pack of drill bits with sizes ranging from #40 to #3 |    0.8 |
| 104 | hammer             | 12oz carpenter's hammer                                 |   0.75 |
| 105 | hammer             | 14oz carpenter's hammer                                 |  0.875 |
| 106 | hammer             | 16oz carpenter's hammer                                 |      1 |
| 107 | rocks              | box of assorted rocks                                   |    5.3 |
| 108 | jacket             | water resistent black wind breaker                      |    0.1 |
| 109 | spare tire         | 24 inch spare tire                                      |   22.2 |
+-----+--------------------+---------------------------------------------------------+--------+
+-------+------------+-----------+----------+------------+
| id    | order_date | purchaser | quantity | product_id |
+-------+------------+-----------+----------+------------+
| 10001 | 2016-01-16 |      1001 |        1 |        102 |
| 10002 | 2016-01-17 |      1002 |        2 |        105 |
| 10003 | 2016-02-19 |      1002 |        2 |        106 |
| 10004 | 2016-02-21 |      1003 |        1 |        107 |
+-------+------------+-----------+----------+------------+
+------------+----------+
| product_id | quantity |
+------------+----------+
|        101 |        3 |
|        102 |        8 |
|        103 |       18 |
|        104 |        4 |
|        105 |        5 |
|        106 |        0 |
|        107 |       44 |
|        108 |        2 |
|        109 |        5 |
+------------+----------+

Then let’s add a new customer.

docker exec -it postgres psql -U postgres -d postgres -c \
"INSERT INTO inventory.customers (first_name, last_name, email) VALUES ('John', 'Doe', 'john.doe@example.com');"

and verify that it is replicated on the destination

docker exec -it mysql mysql -uroot -pdebezium target_db -e "SELECT * FROM migration_inventory_customers;"

There we go! You have now a data replication pipeline migrating data from PostgreSQL to MySQL, in real time, just running a single container!

+------+------------+-----------+-----------------------+
| id   | first_name | last_name | email                 |
+------+------------+-----------+-----------------------+
| 1001 | Sally      | Thomas    | sally.thomas@acme.com |
| 1002 | George     | Bailey    | gbailey@foobar.com    |
| 1003 | Edward     | Walker    | ed@walker.com         |
| 1004 | Anne       | Kretchmar | annek@noanswer.org    |
| 1005 | John       | Doe       | john.doe@example.com  |
+------+------------+-----------+-----------------------+

We recommend keeping an eye on DBZ#1731-Migration of Debezium Server to the Debezium Quarkus Extensions and DBZ#2108-Debezium Server Native, that will enable native build support for DS using the same data migration pipeline with a single native executable.

If you are deploying Debezium on Kubernetes using the Debezium Operator, the same configuration can be expressed using a DebeziumServer custom resource. The operator abstracts much of the operational complexity by translating the custom resource definition into a fully configured DS deployment, allowing you to manage CDC pipelines using Kubernetes-native resources. The spec closely mirrors the underlying DS configuration, so the source and sink settings shown earlier can be mapped almost directly into the custom resource. After installing the Operator on your cluster, you can create the following Custom Resource Definition (CRD).

DebeziumServer custom resource
  apiVersion: debezium.io/v1alpha1
  kind: DebeziumServer
  metadata:
    name: jdbc-sink-example
    namespace: debezium
  spec:
    image: quay.io/debezium/server:latest
    sink:
      type: jdbc
      config:
        connection.url: jdbc:mysql://mysql:3306/target_db
        connection.username: root
        connection.password: debezium
        insert.mode: upsert
        primary.key.mode: record_key
        schema.evolution: basic
        delete.enabled: "true"
    source:
      class: io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector
      config:
        database.hostname: postgres
        database.port: "5432"
        database.user: postgres
        database.password: postgres
        database.dbname: postgres
        topic.prefix: migration
        schema.include.list: inventory
        table.include.list: inventory.customers,inventory.products,inventory.products_on_hand,inventory.orders
    quarkus:
      config:
        log.console.json: "false"

Notice how the source and sink sections correspond directly to the equivalent DS properties. This one-to-one mapping makes it straightforward to transition from a standalone DS deployment to an operator-managed deployment. For a complete description of the DS resource and all available configuration options, refer to the Debezium Server Specification documentation.

Data Integration with Debezium Management Platform

Debezium Platform lets you manage your pipeline with a modern UI, while Debezium orchestrates the entire deployment automatically. Once the platform is installed on your Kubernetes cluster in the debezium-platform namespace, you can create your data replication pipeline ease.

Through the Google Summer of code initiative we have a contributor working to support host based deploy on the Debezium Platform. This means that in the future, you could also deploy the pipeline on VMs, on-prem machines, and the cloud. Keep an eye on https://github.com/debezium/dbz/issues/2085

You can use the following resources to create the source and destination databases. Once applied, a PostgreSQL database acting as the source will be available as postgresql, and another PostgreSQL database acting as the destination will be available as postgresql-dest.

Source PostgreSQL (CDC-enabled, example postgresql database):
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Secret
  metadata:
    name: postgresql-credentials
    namespace: debezium-platform
  type: Opaque
  stringData:
    POSTGRES_USER: debezium
    POSTGRES_PASSWORD: debezium
    POSTGRES_DB: debezium
  ---
  apiVersion: apps/v1
  kind: Deployment
  metadata:
    name: postgresql
  spec:
    replicas: 1
    selector:
      matchLabels:
        app: postgresql
    template:
      metadata:
        labels:
          app: postgresql
      spec:
        containers:
          - name: postgresql
            image: quay.io/debezium/example-postgres:latest
            ports:
              - containerPort: 5432
            envFrom:
              - secretRef:
                  name: postgresql-credentials
  ---
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Service
  metadata:
    name: postgresql
    namespace: debezium-platform
  spec:
    selector:
      app: postgresql
    ports:
      - port: 5432
        targetPort: 5432
Destination PostgreSQL (vanilla, JDBC sink target):
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Secret
  metadata:
    name: postgresql-dest-credentials
    namespace: debezium-platform
  type: Opaque
  stringData:
    POSTGRES_USER: debezium
    POSTGRES_PASSWORD: debezium
  ---
  apiVersion: apps/v1
  kind: Deployment
  metadata:
    name: postgresql-dest
    namespace: debezium-platform
  spec:
    replicas: 1
    selector:
      matchLabels:
        app: postgresql-dest
    template:
      metadata:
        labels:
          app: postgresql-dest
      spec:
        containers:
          - name: postgresql
            image: postgres:16-alpine
            ports:
              - containerPort: 5432
            envFrom:
              - secretRef:
                  name: postgresql-dest-credentials
  ---
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Service
  metadata:
    name: postgresql-dest
    namespace: debezium-platform
  spec:
    selector:
      app: postgresql-dest
    ports:
      - port: 5432
        targetPort: 5432

Let’s now create the connection to the source and the destination database

Create the connection to the source database

Create the connection to the destination database

Then create the source and the destination

Create the source

Create the destination

Once you have all the pieces ready, you can design the pipeline that will replicate data from the source to the destination database

Design the pipeline

and the finally create it

Create the pipeline

It is worth mentioning that you can do the same thing via the REST API with the following

Create source connection:
curl -X POST http://platform.debezium.io/api/connections \
-H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
-d '{
"type": "POSTGRESQL",
"name": "source-postgresql",
"config": {
"hostname": "postgresql",
"port": 5432,
"username": "debezium",
"password": "debezium",
"database": "debezium"
}
}'
Create destination connection:
curl -X POST http://platform.debezium.io/api/connections \
-H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
-d '
{
    "type": "JDBC",
    "name": "dest-postgresql-jdbc",
    "config": {
      "url": "jdbc:postgresql://postgresql-dest.debezium-platform.svc.cluster.local:5432/debezium",
      "username": "debezium",
      "password": "debezium"
    }
}'
Create source (use the connection id from step 1):
curl -X POST http://platform.debezium.io/api/sources \
-H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
-d '
{
    "name": "pg-source",
    "type": "io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector",
    "schema": "dummy",
    "connection": { "id": 1 },
    "config": {
      "schema.include.list": "inventory",
      "table.exclude.list": "inventory.geom,inventory.spatial_ref_sys",
      "topic.prefix": "inventory"
    }
}'
Create destination (use the connection id from step 2):
curl -X POST http://platform.debezium.io/api/destinations \
-H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
-d '
{
    "name": "jdbc-destination",
    "type": "jdbc",
    "schema": "dummy",
    "connection": { "id": 2 },
    "config": {
      "insert.mode": "upsert",
      "primary.key.mode": "record_key",
      "schema.evolution": "basic"
    }
}'
Create pipeline (use the source and destination ids from steps 3 and 4):
curl -X POST http://platform.debezium.io/api/pipelines \
-H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
-d '
{
    "name": "database-migration",
    "source": { "id": 1 },
    "destination": { "id": 1 },
    "logLevel": "INFO"
}'

Conclusion

We have seen how simple it is to build a data migration pipeline without requiring Kafka.

There are still some limitations/differences in the current DS JDBC sink implementation. For example, while Kafka Connect (KC) allows processing to be parallelized by configuring tasks.max with a value greater than 1, this capability is not yet available in DS.

Similarly, if you want to process records from only a specific set of tables, the approach differs from Kafka Connect. Because Kafka provides a durable layer between producers and consumers, consumers can selectively subscribe to specific topics. Debezium Server follows a more direct point-to-point model, where filtering is generally performed at the source rather than the sink. In practice, this means using source connector options such as table.include.list or applying transformations to select the desired events.

If you have specific requirements or feature requests for Debezium Server or the Debezium Management Platform, we’d love to hear from you. Your feedback helps us prioritize what matters most to the community, so feel free to reach out via the mailing list or Zulip chat. For bug reports, feature requests, and enhancement proposals, we encourage you to open an issue in the Debezium issue tracker.
entry.summary: Debezium is often associated with Kafka, and while this was true in the project’s early days, it is no longer the case. We explained in detail, together with several other common misconceptions, in our recent article, "What Nobody Explains About Debezium in 2026 (But Should)". In this article, we’ll build on that discussion by showing the recently added JDBC sink support in Debezium Server (DS) and the Debezium Management Platform (DMP), which opens up Kafka-less data replication and migration scenarios.

entry.title: No More Tuning: Oracle Log Mining Simplified in Debezium 3.6

link.title: No More Tuning: Oracle Log Mining Simplified in Debezium 3.6

entry.content:
If you have ever deployed the Debezium Oracle connector in an environment with bursty workloads, you have probably spent more time than you would like tuning the log.mining.batch.size.*, log.mining.sleep.time.*, and log.mining.scn.gap.detection.* properties. Getting the balance right between peak and quiet periods was, frankly, a losing battle — what worked for your nightly ETL window would over-read during the day, and what worked during the day would fall hopelessly behind at night.

In Debezium 3.6, we replaced this entire mechanism. The connector now selects mining windows based on log file count rather than SCN ranges, controlled by a single new property: log.mining.log.count.min. This post explains why the old approach was so hard to tune, how the new approach works, and what you need to know to migrate.

  • The problem with SCN-based batching

    • How the old algorithm worked

    • Why SCN density made this unpredictable

  • The new approach: log-count-based mining

    • How log-count mining works

    • Tuning the log count

    • Strategy compatibility

  • Configuration migration

    • Properties to remove

    • Before and after

  • Key benefits

  • Wrapping up

The problem with SCN-based batching

How the old algorithm worked

Prior to Debezium 3.6, the Oracle connector used an adaptive batch sizing algorithm to determine the number of rows fetched per LogMiner database call. The algorithm was controlled by a combination of properties that interacted with one another:

log.mining.batch.size.default

The initial number of rows fetched per database call. Default: 20000.

log.mining.batch.size.min

The minimum number of rows fetched per database call. The algorithm would never shrink the batch size below this threshold. Default: 1000.

log.mining.batch.size.max

The maximum number of rows fetched per database call. The algorithm would never grow the batch size above this threshold. Default: 100000.

log.mining.sleep.time.default.ms

The default sleep time between LogMiner polling cycles. Default: 1000.

log.mining.sleep.time.min.ms

The minimum sleep time between polling cycles. Default: 0.

log.mining.sleep.time.max.ms

The maximum sleep time between polling cycles. Default: 3000.

log.mining.sleep.time.increment.ms

The amount by which the sleep time increased or decreased as the connector adapted. Default: 200.

log.mining.scn.gap.detection.gap.size.min

The minimum SCN gap size that would trigger gap detection logic. Default: 1000000.

log.mining.scn.gap.detection.time.interval.max.ms

The maximum time interval used when evaluating SCN gap detection. Default: 20000.

The idea was straightforward: when the connector fell behind, the algorithm would increase the batch size and reduce sleep time so it could process more data per cycle. When the connector caught up to near real-time, it would shrink the batch size and increase sleep time to conserve resources. In theory, this gave the connector the ability to read more data and reduce network latency when it had fallen behind, at the expense of consuming more SGA and JVM memory temporarily, and then use less memory when it was caught up.

In practice, the interaction between these nine properties created a combinatorial tuning problem.

Why SCN density made this unpredictable

The fundamental issue was that SCN ranges do not correspond to a predictable amount of work.

During a nightly batch ETL job, a 1,000,000-SCN window might span dozens of redo log files containing millions of redo entries. The connector would be forced to churn through enormous amounts of log data in each mining pass, overwhelming both LogMiner and the connector’s JVM heap.

During a quiet Sunday afternoon, that same 1,000,000-SCN window might cover a single, partially written redo log with only a handful of changes. The connector would over-read, polling ranges that contained almost no data.

This meant:

  • Tuning for peak volumes (larger batch sizes, shorter sleep times) caused excessive read I/O during quiet periods because the connector would read far more log data than necessary.

  • Tuning for quiet periods (smaller batch sizes, longer sleep times) meant the connector could never catch up during burst peaks because the mining window was too narrow.

  • The interaction between batch size, sleep time, and SCN gap detection made it nearly impossible to find settings that worked well across both scenarios. Adjusting one property often required compensating changes to the others.

This is not a theoretical problem. In a recent post, Nathan Smit from Pepkor NexTech described exactly this scenario — replication lag that persisted despite extensive configuration tuning, ultimately requiring changes to the source database’s loading patterns to reduce redo volume.

The new approach: log-count-based mining

How log-count mining works

In Debezium 3.6, we replaced the SCN-range-based algorithm with one that selects mining windows based on the number of log files per redo thread (dbz#1713). The new property that controls this behavior is:

log.mining.log.count.min

The minimum number of logs per redo thread to include in each mining session. Default: 2.

Instead of defining a mining window by "fetch the next N SCNs worth of changes", the connector now says "mine at least N log files per redo thread". This is a fundamentally different unit of work, and it adapts naturally to the database’s actual activity.

An important detail: the minimum log count only applies when the connector is mining archive logs. Once the connector has caught up and is mining only online redo logs, it always mines from the current read position to the last flushed event in the logs, enabling near real-time event dispatch.

During high-volume periods, redo logs rotate rapidly and archive logs accumulate. The connector reads at least the minimum number of archive logs per redo thread in each pass, which reduces the total number of I/O operations because each pass covers more ground. There is no need to artificially widen an SCN range and risk overwhelming the JVM — log file boundaries define the mining window naturally.

During quiet periods when the connector has caught up to the online redo logs, it mines from its current position to the last flushed event. There is no wasted I/O on empty SCN ranges, no unnecessary polling cycles, and changes are dispatched as soon as they are available.

The key insight is that log file boundaries are a direct reflection of database activity volume. Rapidly rotating archive logs mean the database is busy and the connector is behind — so it batches work by log count. When the connector catches up to the online redo logs, it switches to streaming changes in near real-time. This two-mode behavior adapts to the workload without any manual tuning.

{
    "log.mining.log.count.min": "2"
}

Tuning the log count

In most environments, the default value of 2 is a good starting point.

When the connector is mining archive logs, the total amount of data read per pass per redo thread is:

log.mining.log.count.min  x  redo log file size  =  bytes read per pass per thread

For example, if your redo log files are 500 MB and log.mining.log.count.min is set to 2, the connector will read approximately 1 GB of log data per redo thread per mining pass. If your database has 2 redo threads, that is roughly 2 GB of read I/O per pass.

This makes the property straightforward to reason about:

  • Increase the value if your redo log files are small and rotate frequently. A higher count lets the connector process more logs per session, reducing the overhead of repeated LogMiner start/stop cycles.

  • Decrease the value (down to 1) if your redo log files are very large and you want to limit the amount of data read per pass to reduce peak I/O pressure.

  • Leave the default if your redo log file sizes are moderate. The connector will read a bounded, predictable amount of data per pass and naturally keep pace with the archive log backlog.

Because the redo log file size is fixed by the DBA at the database level, this property gives you a single, predictable lever to control how aggressively the connector works through an archive log backlog — without the cascading side effects of the old batch size, sleep time, and gap detection interactions.

Strategy compatibility

The new log-count-based mining behavior applies to the hybrid and online_catalog mining strategies. The redo_log_catalog strategy is unchanged.

Mining Strategy Behavior

hybrid

Uses log-count-based mining with log.mining.log.count.min.

online_catalog

Uses log-count-based mining with log.mining.log.count.min.

redo_log_catalog

Unchanged. Continues to read all available logs with a fixed one-second poll interval due to its data dictionary flushing requirements.

Configuration migration

Properties to remove

The following properties are now obsolete and should be removed from your connector configuration when upgrading to Debezium 3.6:

  • log.mining.batch.size.default

  • log.mining.batch.size.min

  • log.mining.batch.size.max

  • log.mining.sleep.time.default.ms

  • log.mining.sleep.time.min.ms

  • log.mining.sleep.time.max.ms

  • log.mining.sleep.time.increment.ms

  • log.mining.scn.gap.detection.gap.size.min

  • log.mining.scn.gap.detection.time.interval.max.ms

If any of these properties remain in your connector configuration after upgrading, they will be ignored. We recommend removing them to keep your configuration clean and to avoid confusion during future troubleshooting.

Before and after

Here is what a typical connector configuration looked like before, with properties tuned for a high-volume environment:

{
    "log.mining.batch.size.default": "50000",
    "log.mining.batch.size.min": "5000",
    "log.mining.batch.size.max": "200000",
    "log.mining.sleep.time.default.ms": "500",
    "log.mining.sleep.time.min.ms": "0",
    "log.mining.sleep.time.max.ms": "5000",
    "log.mining.sleep.time.increment.ms": "300",
    "log.mining.scn.gap.detection.gap.size.min": "500000",
    "log.mining.scn.gap.detection.time.interval.max.ms": "30000"
}

And here is the equivalent in Debezium 3.6:

{
    "log.mining.log.count.min": "2"
}

Nine interdependent properties reduced to one.

Key benefits

Reduced read I/O during burst peaks

Reading multiple logs per pass in bounded batches means fewer mining sessions, fewer LogMiner start/stop cycles, and less repeated reading of overlapping log regions. When the database is churning through redo logs during a batch ETL window, the connector keeps pace by processing logs in predictable batches rather than slicing them into arbitrary SCN ranges.

Natural adaptation to workload

The algorithm does not need manual tuning because log file count is an inherent signal of database activity volume. Large, rapidly rotating logs mean high activity; small, slowly rotating logs mean low activity. The connector responds to this signal automatically.

Simpler configuration

Approximately nine interdependent properties have been replaced by a single, intuitive setting that most users will not need to change from its default value. This dramatically reduces the time spent on initial configuration and ongoing tuning.

More predictable behavior

Mining throughput is no longer subject to the unpredictable relationship between SCN ranges and actual data volume. A mining session that processes one or more log files will do a consistent, bounded amount of work regardless of how many SCNs those logs happen to span.

Wrapping up

The log mining batch sizing algorithm has been one of the most difficult aspects of the Oracle connector to configure correctly. By moving from SCN-range-based batching to log-file-count-based mining, Debezium 3.6 eliminates the need for the complex, environment-specific tuning that users have struggled with for years.

The full details of this change can be found in dbz#1713. If you are upgrading from an earlier version, review your connector configuration and remove the obsolete batch.size, sleep.time, and scn.gap.detection properties as described in the migration section above.

We would love to hear about your experience with this change. If you have questions or feedback, please reach out on the mailing list or Zulip chat. You can also find details about everything else in Debezium 3.6 in the release notes.
