entry.title: Debezium 3.6.0.Beta1 Released
entry.content:
We’re excited to announce the release of Debezium 3.6.0.Beta1, which brings a wealth of new features and improvements to the Debezium ecosystem.

This release upgrades to Apache Kafka 4.3, introduces an incubating Apache Fluss sink adapter for Debezium Server, adds an incubating YashanDB source connector, and deprecates the redo_log_catalog Oracle mining strategy. On the operations side, the Debezium Operator now supports OpenTelemetry configuration and configurable image pull policies. Additional highlights include PostgreSQL publication-level skipped operations propagation, a new message-size-aware column truncation feature for Vitess, and a compatibility fix for MongoDB 8.0+ containers on recent Linux kernels.

  • Breaking changes

  • New features and improvements

  • Other changes

Breaking changes

With any new release of software, there can be breaking changes. This release is no exception, so let’s discuss the major changes you should be aware of before upgrading to Debezium 3.6.0.Beta1

Debezium for Oracle

Deprecation of the "redo_log_catalog" mining strategy

The redo_log_catalog mining strategy is now deprecated and will be removed in a future major release.

This strategy relied on Oracle’s redo log for catalog and dictionary information rather than the online catalog, leading to increased complexity, higher memory consumption, slower session startup, and increased redo log generation rates, that are often not sustainable in large enterprise systems.

Users still using the redo_log_catalog mining strategy should plan to migrate to the online_catalog or hybrid strategies, which provides better performance and more consistent behavior. (dbz#1693)

Debezium for SQL Server

Unavailable value placeholder support for large column types

When an UPDATE occurs on a table with VARBINARY(MAX), VARCHAR(MAX), or NVARCHAR(MAX) columns, SQL Server CDC assigns NULL to columns whose values were not changed.

The connector now uses the unavailable.value.placeholder for these unchanged large-column values, aligning the behavior with how PostgreSQL TOAST columns and Oracle BLOB/CLOB columns are handled. This allows consumers to distinguish between a column that was explicitly set to NULL and one that simply was not modified. (dbz#1164)

Users who are capturing such column types should verify consumer ingestion of placeholder values.

New Features and Improvements

The following covers all new features and improvements, grouped by connector component area.

Debezium Core

Debezium for Oracle

Debezium for PostgreSQL

Debezium for SQL Server

Debezium Operator

Debezium Platform

Debezium Server

Debezium for CockroachDB

Debezium for Vitess

Debezium for YashanDB

Container Images

Build Infrastructure

Testcontainers

Debezium Core

Upgrade to Apache Kafka 4.3

Debezium now builds against and ships with Apache Kafka 4.3.0. This upgrade brings the latest Kafka improvements and ensures compatibility with the newest Kafka runtime for users running the latest broker versions. (dbz#1987)

Debezium for Oracle

Optional removal of non-critical LogMiner metadata columns

The Oracle connector now allows non-critical metadata columns such as CLIENT_ID, USERNAME, COMMIT_TIMESTAMP, and START_TIMESTAMP to be excluded from LogMiner queries.

Removing these columns can improve query performance and reduces the overall memory footprint of the connector. Evaluate whether these fields are needed for downstream consumers before excluding them from the query. (dbz#1663)

Debezium for PostgreSQL

Propagation of skipped operations to PostgreSQL publications

The PostgreSQL connector now propagates the skipped.operations configuration into the publication definition when creating or updating publications.

Previously, publications always published all operation types regardless of the connector’s skip configuration, resulting in potentially unnecessary WAL entries for operations that Debezium would later discard. With this change, the publication’s publish option is set to match the connector configuration, reducing replication traffic and processing overhead at the PostgreSQL level. (dbz#1970)

Debezium for SQL Server

New when_needed_no_data snapshot mode

A new when_needed_no_data snapshot mode is now available for the SQL Server connector.

This mode combines the automatic recovery behavior of when_needed with the lightweight approach of no_data, performing a schema-only snapshot without emitting row-level data when the connector detects that its offsets are no longer available on the server. This eliminates the need to manually delete offsets or persistent volumes when LSN positions expire. (dbz#1513)

Set-based LSN-to-timestamp resolution for improved query performance

The SQL Server connector now uses a LEFT JOIN on the cdc.lsn_time_mapping table instead of calling the fn_cdc_map_lsn_to_time() scalar function per row.

This set-based approach resolves timestamps in a single operation rather than row-by-row, significantly improving CDC query performance on high-volume tables. The change only affects the FUNCTION data query mode and produces identical output. (dbz#1915)

Debezium Operator

Configurable image pull policy in the DebeziumServer CRD

The Debezium Operator now supports specifying an ImagePullPolicy in the DebeziumServer custom resource definition via spec.runtime.templates.container.imagePullPolicy. This allows users to control when container images are pulled, avoiding unnecessary pulls from the registry on every pod creation and reducing startup latency in environments where images are already cached locally. (dbz#1591)

OpenTelemetry monitoring support

The Debezium Operator now supports configuring the OpenTelemetry Java Agent on Debezium Server instances through the DebeziumServer custom resource.

Users can enable OpenTelemetry-based monitoring via spec.runtime.metrics.opentelemetry, specifying the collector endpoint and enabling automatic injection of environment variables and resource attributes such as service name and connector type. This provides a modern alternative to the existing JMX Exporter configuration for observability. (dbz#1896)

Debezium Platform

MongoDB source connector support

The Debezium Platform now supports validating and creating MongoDB source connections. Users can configure MongoDB as a source directly through the platform UI, expanding the set of supported database types beyond relational databases and bringing MongoDB CDC management into the unified platform experience. (dbz#1871)

Dynamic catalog API integration for connector listing

The Debezium Platform UI now uses the catalog API to dynamically list available connectors instead of relying on a static file. This ensures that newly registered connector types are automatically discovered and displayed, keeping the platform interface consistent with the actual set of available connectors. (dbz#1920)

Schema descriptor-driven destination connector forms

Destination connectors in the Debezium Platform now render their configuration forms using schema descriptors instead of free-text fields. This provides a more structured and user-friendly configuration experience with proper field types, validation, and documentation directly in the UI. (dbz#1921)

Simplified signal verification payload

The signal verification request payload in the Debezium Platform has been updated to accept a connectionId instead of the full connection properties. This simplifies the API contract by referencing an existing connection rather than requiring all connection details to be re-specified in each verification request. (dbz#1937)

Debezium Server

Incubating Apache Fluss sink adapter

Apache Fluss is a streaming storage system designed for real-time analytics and AI workloads in Lakehouse architectures.

An incubating sink adapter for Apache Fluss is now available in Debezium Server. This integration enables a Kafka-less CDC pipeline from source databases directly into Fluss, simplifying the architecture and reducing operational overhead for users who want to feed both real-time and batch analytics from a single pipeline. (dbz#1840)

Debezium for CockroachDB

BeanRegistry integration

The CockroachDB connector now registers its key components—such as the configuration class, JDBC connection, schema, and value converters—in the BeanRegistry, aligning it with the pattern used by other Debezium connectors. This ensures the connector properly uses the core QueueServiceProvider and other default registered services, enabling a more consistent and extensible architecture. (dbz#1983)

Debezium for Vitess

Automatic column truncation based on maximum message size

The Vitess connector now supports automatic column truncation to ensure produced messages stay within a configurable maximum size.

This eliminates the manual effort of resizing and updating truncation settings as schemas evolve, preventing message size violations on downstream systems such as Kafka. The connector dynamically calculates truncation thresholds and applies them across all applicable columns. (dbz#1879)

Debezium for YashanDB

New incubating YashanDB source connector

Debezium now includes an incubating source connector for YashanDB, a relational database that provides an XStream-like CDC interface called YStream.

The connector supports full snapshots via JDBC with concurrent table splitting by ROWID for improved performance, and incremental streaming via YStream’s logical log parsing. This contribution from the YashanDB team enables seamless data connectivity between YashanDB and the broader Debezium ecosystem. (dbz#1850)

Container Images

Oracle Query Tool added to the tooling image

The Debezium tooling container image now includes the Debezium Oracle Query Tool, a CLI utility for fetching LogMiner data from Oracle systems. This tool joins the existing set of utilities such as kcctl and pgcli already shipped in the tooling image, providing a convenient way to inspect and debug Oracle LogMiner queries directly from the container. (dbz#1952)

Build Infrastructure

ArchUnit enforcement for component descriptor interfaces

An ArchUnit rule now verifies that all configurable components implement the required ConfigDescriptor interface. This build-time enforcement prevents components from being inadvertently omitted from the generated descriptor catalog, and the rule is reusable by any repository that depends on debezium-parent. (dbz#1979)

Testcontainers

Compatibility fix for MongoDB 8.0+ with Linux kernel 6.19+

An update to Linux kernel 6.19 and later introduced a compatibility issue that could prevent MongoDB 8.0+ containers from starting correctly. The test container images now include the GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.pthread.rseq=1 environment variable workaround, ensuring reliable MongoDB container startup on hosts running recent Linux kernels. (dbz#1945)

Other fixes

  • Connector context MDC tag is missing in logs produced in the ChangeEventSourceCoordinator thread (dbz#1933)

  • NullPointerException in ApproximateStructSizeCalculator when finished-partition cleanup dispatches a null-offset heartbeat (dbz#1944)

  • MySQL connector fails to parse DDL when SRID follows NULL/NOT NULL (dbz#1510)

  • Full database snapshot occurs when snapshot mode is when_needed (dbz#1942)

  • Incorrect pg_stat_replication.reply_time calculation (dbz#1950)

  • Snapshot fails at step 7 with "Cannot execute without committing" (dbz#1976)

  • Snapshot fails with "Failed reading CURRENT_TIMESTAMP" when connections go stale during stage 6 (dbz#1977)

  • JDBC sink connector errors when -infinity is provided for a timestamptz column that is not the first row in a batch (dbz#1658)

  • Debezium Server JDBC sink descriptors are not generated (dbz#1961)

  • Fix artifactId in the Quarkus Extensions documentation (dbz#1972)

  • Unintended scroll in the card UI for unusually long names in catalog listing (dbz#1967)

  • Pipeline creation fails on Debezium Platform (dbz#1990)

  • Build of Debezium Server fails (dbz#1962)

  • Table discovery only scans cockroachdb.schema.name and ignores schema.include.list (dbz#1973)

  • Typed column DEFAULT values rejected because DefaultValueConverter is null (dbz#1975)

  • Document uppercase schema and table name behavior causing topic creation failures for Oracle (dbz#1892)

  • Update documentation with quantile metrics (dbz#1903)

  • Use the default storage class in testing persistent volume claims (dbz#1971)

In total, 50 issues were resolved in Debezium 3.6.0.Beta1. The list of changes can also be found in our release notes.

A big thank you to all the contributors from the community who worked diligently on this release:
Alvar Viana Gomez, Atsushi Torikoshi, Cao Ba Huong, Chris Cranford, Daniele Licini, Davyd Eliosidze, Giovanni Panice, Indra Shukla, Jakub Małek, Jiri Pechanec, Lars M. Johansson, Mario Fiore Vitale, Matei Alexandru Gatin, Mohammad Akhil, Mohnish, Nathan Smit, Philippe Camus, Thomas Thornton, Tomoyuki Nakamura, Tony Nyurkin, Vincenzo Santonastaso, Virag Tripathi, and Vojtech Juranek!

entry.title: What Nobody Explains About Debezium in 2026 (But Should)

link.title: What Nobody Explains About Debezium in 2026 (But Should)

entry.content:
Teams evaluating Change Data Capture (CDC) tools often encounter comparison articles with titles like "Top Debezium Alternatives in 2026" or "Why We Moved Away from Debezium." These articles can be useful starting points for evaluation, but many rely on characterizations that reflect older deployment patterns rather than Debezium’s current capabilities.

Debezium is not the right fit for every team or every use case, and we will be upfront about that in this post. Different CDC tools optimize for different goals: some prioritize turnkey SaaS experiences, others focus on tightly integrated transformation pipelines, and Debezium optimizes for openness, composability, database breadth, and deployment flexibility. Understanding these tradeoffs is more useful than debating which tool is "best."

This post addresses common questions that arise during CDC evaluations, with an honest look at where Debezium fits and where other approaches might serve your team better.

Deployment models and the Kafka question

One of the most common questions during CDC evaluations is whether Debezium requires Apache Kafka. This characterization reflects earlier deployment patterns. Debezium is a Change Data Capture platform, and Apache Kafka Connect is one deployment model, not a requirement.

For many teams, Kafka Connect remains the preferred deployment model, not because it is the only option, but because of the capabilities it provides.

Why teams choose Kafka Connect

Deploying Debezium on Kafka Connect is not just a legacy pattern. It’s a deliberate architectural choice that unlocks a rich set of capabilities:

  • A vast ecosystem of sink connectors. Kafka Connect has hundreds of production-grade sink connectors: JDBC sinks for relational databases, Elasticsearch, S3, Snowflake, BigQuery, and many more. Deploying Debezium as a Kafka Connect source connector means you can pair it with any of these sinks without writing integration code.

  • Built-in high availability and fault tolerance. Kafka Connect’s distributed mode handles worker failures, automatic task rebalancing, and offset management out of the box. Your CDC pipeline keeps running even if a node goes down.

  • Scalable distributed processing. Kafka Connect can distribute work across a cluster of workers, balancing load automatically as connectors and tasks are added or removed.

For organizations already using Kafka Connect, or those whose use case benefits from these capabilities, it remains an excellent deployment model and one that many teams actively prefer.

Other deployment options

For teams that don’t need the full Kafka ecosystem, or that prefer a lighter-weight deployment, Debezium offers first-class alternatives that use the same battle-tested source connectors.

Debezium Server is a standalone, ready-to-run application that provides native connectivity with other streaming platforms and messaging systems: Amazon Kinesis, Google Cloud Pub/Sub, Apache Pulsar, Redis Streams, RabbitMQ, HTTP webhooks, and more. If your organization is already invested in one of these ecosystems, Debezium Server lets you bring CDC to that platform directly, using the same proven source connectors, without introducing Kafka as an additional layer.

Debezium Platform takes this further, providing an operator-based deployment model that manages the full lifecycle of Debezium connectors, including configuration, scaling, and health management, all without requiring any Kafka ecosystem components.

The perception that Debezium requires Kafka persists in part because many tutorials were written before these options existed and are still widely shared. In many deployments today, Kafka is not part of the architecture at all.

A more useful framing is: "do I need the capabilities that Kafka provides?" If you do, Kafka Connect is a powerful deployment model with a rich ecosystem. If you don’t, Debezium Server and Platform give you the same CDC engine without the additional infrastructure.

Setup complexity and getting started

Some evaluation articles describe getting Debezium running in production as a multi-day or multi-week effort requiring extensive component configuration. Historically, Kafka Connect deployments did involve more moving parts, and that shaped perceptions. The landscape looks different today, particularly with Debezium Server.

Here is what a basic Debezium Server setup actually involves. We’ll use MySQL as the example, since it also requires schema history storage, which makes it a good illustration of a realistic configuration.

docker run -d --name debezium -p 8080:8080 \
  -v debezium-data:/debezium/data \
  -e DEBEZIUM_SOURCE_CONNECTOR_CLASS=io.debezium.connector.mysql.MySqlConnector \
  -e DEBEZIUM_SOURCE_DATABASE_HOSTNAME=your-db-host \
  -e DEBEZIUM_SOURCE_DATABASE_PORT=3306 \
  -e DEBEZIUM_SOURCE_DATABASE_USER=debezium \
  -e DEBEZIUM_SOURCE_DATABASE_PASSWORD=secret \
  -e DEBEZIUM_SOURCE_TOPIC_PREFIX=myapp \
  -e DEBEZIUM_SOURCE_OFFSET_STORAGE=io.debezium.storage.file.history.FileOffsetBackingStore \
  -e DEBEZIUM_SOURCE_OFFSET_STORAGE_FILE_FILENAME=/debezium/data/offsets.dat \
  -e DEBEZIUM_SOURCE_SCHEMA_HISTORY_INTERNAL=io.debezium.storage.file.history.FileSchemaHistory \
  -e DEBEZIUM_SOURCE_SCHEMA_HISTORY_INTERNAL_FILE_FILENAME=/debezium/data/schema-history.dat \
  -e DEBEZIUM_SINK_TYPE=kinesis \
  -e DEBEZIUM_SINK_KINESIS_REGION=us-east-1 \
  quay.io/debezium/server:3.5

Or, if you prefer docker-compose, a minimal docker-compose.yml for the same setup looks like this:

services:
  debezium:
    image: quay.io/debezium/server:3.5
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    volumes:
      - ./conf:/debezium/conf
      - debezium-data:/debezium/data
    environment:
      - DEBEZIUM_SOURCE_CONNECTOR_CLASS=io.debezium.connector.mysql.MySqlConnector
      - DEBEZIUM_SOURCE_DATABASE_HOSTNAME=your-db-host
      - DEBEZIUM_SOURCE_DATABASE_PORT=3306
      - DEBEZIUM_SOURCE_DATABASE_USER=debezium
      - DEBEZIUM_SOURCE_DATABASE_PASSWORD=secret
      - DEBEZIUM_SOURCE_TOPIC_PREFIX=myapp
      - DEBEZIUM_SOURCE_OFFSET_STORAGE=io.debezium.storage.file.history.FileOffsetBackingStore
      - DEBEZIUM_SOURCE_OFFSET_STORAGE_FILE_FILENAME=/debezium/data/offsets.dat
      - DEBEZIUM_SOURCE_SCHEMA_HISTORY_INTERNAL=io.debezium.storage.file.history.FileSchemaHistory
      - DEBEZIUM_SOURCE_SCHEMA_HISTORY_INTERNAL_FILE_FILENAME=/debezium/data/schema-history.dat
      - DEBEZIUM_SINK_TYPE=kinesis
      - DEBEZIUM_SINK_KINESIS_REGION=us-east-1
volumes:
  debezium-data:

That is the entire deployment: configure your source connection and your sink destination, and you have a complete CDC pipeline with one unit of deployment.

An important distinction: configuring your database correctly, enabling logical replication on PostgreSQL, configuring the correct binlog_format on MySQL, or setting up the LogMiner permissions on Oracle, does require careful attention. These steps are not unique to Debezium; any CDC tool that reads from transaction logs requires the same database-level setup. Debezium’s documentation covers each database thoroughly.

Teams often encounter setup complexity that is inherent to CDC itself rather than specific to Debezium. Distinguishing between the two is important when comparing tools.

There is also a deployment path worth highlighting: embedding Debezium directly into your application.

For Java developers: the Debezium Quarkus Extensions

If you are already building Java applications, there is another option that sidesteps the infrastructure question entirely: the Debezium Quarkus Extensions.

Quarkus is a Kubernetes-native Java framework designed for building cloud-native applications, with a focus on fast startup, low memory footprint, and a developer-friendly experience. The Debezium Quarkus Extensions let you embed Debezium directly inside any Quarkus-based application, running CDC as part of your existing service rather than as a separate piece of infrastructure.

For teams already building Quarkus services, especially those implementing patterns like the outbox where CDC is tightly coupled to the application, this can be the most natural way to adopt Debezium. Quarkus offers a rich ecosystem out of the box: dependency injection, configuration management, live reload in dev mode, and native compilation with GraalVM if you need it. Adding CDC to a Quarkus application is as straightforward as adding any other extension:

<dependency>
  <groupId>io.debezium.quarkus</groupId>
  <artifactId>quarkus-debezium-mysql</artifactId>
</dependency>

From there, Debezium participates in the standard Quarkus application lifecycle. Configuration lives in application.properties, alongside the rest of your application’s configuration. Change events are consumed as CDI events. The entire Quarkus developer experience, including dev services that spin up databases automatically for local development, is available.

Other embedded options

Quarkus is not the only way to embed Debezium into an application.

  • Spring Integration provides first-class Debezium support, letting Spring Boot applications consume change events through familiar Spring messaging channels. For teams already in the Spring ecosystem, this is a natural fit.

  • Apache Camel includes Debezium components for each supported database, letting teams capture change events as part of Camel integration routes. For organizations already using Camel for enterprise integration, this provides a familiar way to incorporate CDC into existing workflows.

  • Debezium Engine is the underlying embedding API that powers all of these integrations. If you don’t use a specific framework, you can embed Debezium directly into any Java application with a few lines of code and full control over how events are consumed.

  • PyDebezium brings Debezium’s CDC capabilities to Python applications, opening the door for data engineering teams and Python-first organizations.

Why this matters for setup complexity

The setup experience looks very different when Debezium is just another dependency in a project your team already knows how to build, test, and deploy. There is no separate process to operate, no separate configuration format to learn, and no context switch between your application and your CDC pipeline.

Whether you embed via Quarkus, Spring, the Debezium Engine directly, or even Python, the point is the same: Debezium adapts to your stack rather than requiring you to adopt a new one.

Transformation capabilities

A common question in CDC evaluations is whether Debezium provides sufficient transformation support. The answer depends on what your use case requires and how you think about where transformations belong in your architecture.

Debezium is designed as a CDC solution, not a general-purpose transformation engine. This is a deliberate architectural choice: do one thing extremely well, and compose cleanly with tools that handle the next stage. Some CDC tools take the opposite approach, building transformation capabilities directly into the platform. Both approaches have merit, and which one fits better depends on your team’s architecture and preferences.

For transformation needs within the CDC layer, Debezium’s Single Message Transforms (SMTs) cover significant ground out of the box:

  • Routing events to different topics based on content

  • Extracting only the "after" state of a record (flattening the event envelope)

  • Filtering events by table or operation type

  • Masking or replacing sensitive column values

  • Converting data types

  • Adding metadata fields to events

  • Generating vector embeddings from change events using AI models for semantic search and RAG pipelines

Debezium also supports any Kafka Connect-compatible SMT, not just its own. The broader Kafka ecosystem of transformations is available across all Debezium deployment options: Debezium Server, the embedded Engine, the Quarkus Extensions, and every other part of the portfolio. This gives you access to a wide library of existing community transforms regardless of how you deploy.

For teams that need heavier in-flight processing, such as complex joins, aggregations, or conditional routing across multiple change event streams, the natural approach is integrating Debezium with a stream processor like Apache Flink or Kafka Streams. These tools are purpose-built for complex event processing, and Debezium’s Kafka Connect deployment makes that integration straightforward.

For teams using Debezium’s embedded deployment options, such as the Quarkus Extensions, Spring Integration, or the Debezium Engine directly, transformation capabilities are effectively unlimited. You have the full power of your programming language available to process, enrich, or transform change events however your use case demands, with no constraints imposed by a plugin API.

Monitoring and observability

Debezium does not include a built-in web interface for monitoring connectors. This is a real gap for teams that expect a turnkey monitoring experience, and it is worth acknowledging directly.

What Debezium does provide is comprehensive metrics exposure. Debezium exposes a rich set of JMX metrics covering connector status, transaction log position, event counts, processing rates, and lag. When paired with Prometheus JMX Exporter and Grafana, you get production-grade observability with dashboards the community has built and shared. The Debezium monitoring example provides a ready-to-run setup with Prometheus and Grafana pre-configured, so you can see what this looks like in practice.

Setting up this observability stack is a real step. The distinction between "no monitoring" and "requires a standard observability stack" is important. The Prometheus and Grafana combination is the industry standard for monitoring Java-based distributed systems, and Debezium integrates naturally with that ecosystem. Teams already running this stack will find Debezium metrics straightforward to add. Teams without an existing observability stack will need to account for that setup.

For teams running Debezium on Kubernetes, the Debezium Operator integrates with standard Kubernetes observability tooling, and connector health is surfaced through standard resource status fields.

This is also an area where the project is actively investing. Debezium Platform is gaining native metrics and monitoring support, built in rather than bolted on, so that operators will have first-class observability with the ability for Debezium to provide the entire stack for you. That work is in progress and reflects the project’s commitment to reducing operational friction.

When Debezium may not be the best fit

Choosing the right CDC tool means understanding where each option’s strengths align with your team’s needs. Debezium is not the best fit for every situation, and we would rather be direct about that than leave you to discover it after investing time in an evaluation.

You want a fully managed, end-to-end SaaS workflow. Debezium is an open-source project, and running it yourself means you are responsible for operations, monitoring, and upgrades. Debezium Platform is actively reducing that operational burden, and several vendors offer managed CDC services built on Debezium, so managed options do exist. But if your primary requirement is a turnkey SaaS experience with no operational responsibility, tools that are built as managed services from the ground up may be a more natural fit.

You prefer a tightly integrated transformation and runtime platform. Some CDC tools bundle transformation, orchestration, and delivery into a single integrated platform. If your team values that kind of opinionated, all-in-one experience over the flexibility of composing separate tools, those platforms may align better with your workflow.

Your team has no existing JVM or distributed systems operational experience. Debezium runs on the Java Virtual Machine (JVM). PyDebezium makes it possible to consume change events from Python applications, and the Debezium Quarkus Extensions provide GraalVM native compilation, removing the need to install a JVM at runtime.

Even so, the underlying engine is a JVM-based system. When something goes wrong in production, and in any distributed system something eventually will, troubleshooting and bug reporting will benefit from at least some familiarity with that ecosystem. If your operations team has none, there will be a learning curve.

You have small-scale CDC needs where deployment simplicity outweighs flexibility. For straightforward, small-scale CDC scenarios where you don’t need Debezium’s range of deployment options, database support, or ecosystem integrations, a simpler tool with fewer choices may get you to production faster.

How Debezium fits modern CDC architectures

Debezium’s design philosophy prioritizes composability, openness, and integration into existing data ecosystems rather than providing a single tightly coupled platform. This means teams assemble their CDC pipelines from components that fit their architecture, choosing their deployment model, their messaging infrastructure, their transformation layer, and their observability stack.

That composability comes with tradeoffs. It requires more architectural decisions upfront compared to an opinionated platform, and teams need to be comfortable with that responsibility. For organizations that value flexibility, ecosystem portability, and the ability to evolve their architecture independently, it is a significant advantage.

Today, Debezium offers a range of deployment options to fit different architectures and team needs:

  • Kafka Connect for teams that want the full ecosystem of sink connectors, built-in high availability, durable history, and scalable distributed processing.

  • Debezium Server for streaming changes directly to platforms like Kinesis, Pub/Sub, Pulsar, or RabbitMQ, with a single container and no Kafka dependency.

  • Debezium Platform for operator-managed deployments with lifecycle management, scaling, and health monitoring.

  • Embedded via Quarkus, Spring, or the Debezium Engine for teams that want CDC as part of their application, with the full power of their programming language for processing events.

  • PyDebezium for Python-first teams and data engineering workflows.

Transformations are handled by a rich set of SMTs out of the box, including AI-powered embeddings, and any Kafka Connect-compatible SMT works across all deployment options. Monitoring integrates with standard JVM observability tooling, and Debezium Platform is actively investing in built-in observability.

Debezium has been in active development since 2015, is battle-tested in production across a wide range of industries, and is backed by an engaged open-source community. That maturity matters when you’re choosing infrastructure your data pipelines will depend on.

Different organizations value different tradeoffs, and evaluations should reflect the capabilities and deployment models available today rather than assumptions carried over from earlier generations of CDC tooling. We hope this gives you a more complete and current picture for your evaluation.

If you’d like to try Debezium yourself, the Debezium Server quickstart is the fastest way to see it in action, and our community is ready to help you with the first steps.

Have questions or want to discuss? Join the conversation in the Debezium community.

These articles can be useful starting points for evaluation, but many rely on characterizations that reflect older deployment patterns rather than Debezium’s current capabilities. Different CDC tools optimize for different goals: some prioritize turnkey SaaS experiences, others focus on tightly integrated transformation pipelines, and Debezium optimizes for openness, composability, database breadth, and deployment flexibility. entry.title: Debezium 3.6.0.Alpha2 Released
entry.content:
We’re pleased to announce the release of Debezium 3.6.0.Alpha2, the second development preview in the 3.6 series, delivering a range of new features, improvements, and bug fixes. This release introduces quantile metrics across all connectors, JDBC sink support for Debezium Server, and Debezium Platform enhancements including configurable labels and server images. Other highlights include a SQL Server CDC column filter toggle, a Kafka 4.2 upgrade, a Google Cloud BOM update, and the removal of the deprecated MySQL and MariaDB never snapshot mode. Read on for the full details!

  • Breaking changes

  • New features and improvements

  • Other changes

Breaking changes

With any new release of software, there can be breaking changes. This release is no exception, so let’s discuss the major changes you should be aware of before upgrading to Debezium 3.6.0.Alpha2.

Debezium for MySQL

Removal of NEVER snapshot mode

The never option has been removed from the snapshot.mode configuration property for MySQL and MariaDB connectors. This mode, which replayed all available binlog events rather than taking an initial snapshot, was deprecated during the Debezium 3.0 release. Users who currently specify snapshot.mode=never will encounter a configuration error at startup and should migrate to one of the remaining valid snapshot modes. (dbz#1832)

New Features and Improvements

The following covers all new features and improvements, grouped by connector component area.

Debezium Core

Debezium for MySQL

Debezium for SQL Server

Debezium Platform

Debezium Server

Debezium Core

Kafka 4.2.0

Debezium now builds against and supports Apache Kafka 4.2.0. This upgrade brings the latest Kafka client improvements, bug fixes, and protocol enhancements to all Debezium connectors. (dbz#1651)

Quantile metrics

Quantile metrics provide statistical distribution data for metrics such as latencies and other time-based measurements. Originally available only in the Spanner connector, these metrics and their underlying statistics classes have been incorporated into Debezium core, making quantile metrics available across all connectors for more granular performance monitoring and analysis. (dbz#1417)

Debezium for MySQL

Migration to ANTLR Oracle MySQL grammar

The MySQL DDL parser has been migrated from the Positive Technologies MySQL grammar to the ANTLR Oracle MySQL grammar. The Positive Technologies grammar is no longer maintained and is being deprecated by the ANTLR team, making this migration necessary to ensure continued parser updates and compatibility with newer MySQL syntax. (dbz#1216)

If you encounter any issues, you can revert to the legacy DDL parser by setting ddl.parser.type to legacy. The legacy DDL parser will be removed in a future build of Debezium.

Debezium for SQL Server

Internal property to toggle CDC column filters

When CDC is enabled for a SQL Server table with only a subset of columns included in the capture instance, snapshots previously respected the CDC column filter, omitting columns not tracked by CDC. This can cause issues for snapshot-only migrations or when columns are added after CDC was initially enabled.

A new internal configuration property, internal.change.column.filter.override, can be set to true to override this behavior so that all table columns are included during snapshot regardless of the CDC capture configuration. (dbz#1830)

Debezium Platform

Labels for DebeziumServer custom resources

When the Debezium Platform conductor creates a DebeziumServer custom resource for a new pipeline, it now supports passing custom labels to the CR. This enables users to view and manage these resources in tools like ArgoCD that rely on labels for resource discovery and visualization. (dbz#1768)

Configurable Debezium Server image

The Debezium Platform now permits specifying which Debezium Server container image to use when creating a DebeziumServer CRD through a new application property on the conductor. A default value is also configurable via the Helm chart’s values.yaml, providing consistency with how conductor and stage images are already specified. (dbz#1826)

Debezium Server

Google Cloud BOM update to 26.79.0

The Google Cloud Libraries BOM dependency has been updated from 26.17.0 to 26.79.0, bringing improvements in reliability and resilience for cloud-based sinks such as Pub/Sub. This update helps improve network resilience when pushing messages to Google Cloud services. (dbz#1822)

JDBC sink support

The JDBC sink connector, previously available only as a Kafka Connect sink, is now supported as a native Debezium Server sink. This enables lightweight database-to-database replication without requiring a Kafka Connect deployment, supporting all existing JDBC sink capabilities including upsert and insert modes, delete handling, schema evolution, and batch processing across multiple database dialects. (dbz#1842)

Other fixes

  • Duplicate dependency in debezium-embedded module (dbz#1855)

  • Fix intermittent failure in TransactionMetadataIT by adding waitForStreamingRunning before CDC operations (dbz#1935)

  • Conditional incremental snapshot state lost on interruption (dbz#1807)

  • MySqlChunkedSnapshotIT shouldSnapshotMultipleTablesChunkedWithVaryingRowCounts is flaky (dbz#1760)

  • HybridMiningStrategyIT fails after updating to Kafka 4.2 (dbz#1874)

  • Document ORA-26913 RAC instance pinning issue for XStream adapter (dbz#1880)

  • OracleConnectorIT shouldFailWhenConverterThrowsExceptionForValue fails randomly (dbz#1893)

  • Default values with escaped enum types do not show up (dbz#1334)

  • flush_lsn may not advance with lsn.flush.mode=connector_and_driver when only unmonitored tables are updated (dbz#1605)

  • Refactor CDC/TransactionEngine (dbz#1889)

  • PipelineMapper does not handle SQL Server-specific database.names property (dbz#1828)

  • Add more supporting TRL unit tests and E2E tests for the updated source connection flow (dbz#1814)

  • Stage UI does not render multiple booleans in connection values correctly (dbz#1838)

  • Connection edit flow results in failure for properties with dot (.) in name (dbz#1844)

  • Destination edit fails due to required fields missing from the payload (dbz#1845)

  • PipelineMapperTest fails for an unmocked dependency (dbz#1853)

  • Disable the signalling setup when no connection is selected in the source dropdown (dbz#1908)

  • Stage UI not working well on Safari (dbz#1911)

  • Update Pulsar Client to 4.2.1 (dbz#1865)

  • Partition in BatchEvent can be null (dbz#1854)

  • Document OCI JDBC driver requirement and libaio dependency for XStream adapter (dbz#1856)

  • Add database.service.name configuration property for Oracle (dbz#1885)

  • Move MongoDB image in debezium-testing-testcontainers to Quay registry (dbz#1846)

  • Add summary report to test (dbz#1881)

  • Log test class and test name on each invocation (dbz#1882)

  • Update Connect cluster version to the same version as Kafka cluster (dbz#1890)

  • Update Kafka Connect logger to log4j2 format (dbz#1891)

In total, 36 issues were resolved in Debezium 3.6.0.Alpha2. The list of changes can also be found in our release notes.

entry.title: Debezium welcomes its Google Summer of Code 2026 Contributors!

link.title: Debezium welcomes its Google Summer of Code 2026 Contributors!

entry.content:
We’re excited to share the next milestone in Debezium’s Google Summer of Code 2026 journey: our contributors have been selected, and the community bonding period has officially started! 🎉

Earlier this year, we announced that Debezium would participate in Google Summer of Code 2026 as part of the JBoss Community organization, offering project ideas focused on change data capture, vector databases, Quarkus, AI/ML, developer tooling, and the Debezium platform. Since then, we’ve had many interesting conversations with prospective contributors, reviewed proposals, and worked together to select the projects that will move forward this year.

The official GSoC 2026 timeline announced accepted contributors on April 30th, followed by the community bonding period from May 1st to May 24th. Coding will officially begin on May 25th.

Meet Our GSoC 2026 Contributors

We’re happy to welcome the contributors to the Debezium community for the following projects:

Debezium CLI

summary: Debezium CLI would provide developers and operators with a streamlined way to create, manage, and monitor CDC pipelines across data systems.

Contributor: Binayak Das

Proposal: link

About the contributor: Binayak Das is a Computer Science and Engineering student from India very interested in Java backend systems, AI/ML, developer tooling and open source software. He has contributed to organisations such as Scala3, OpenMRS and Debezium since in his first year of college.

Mentors: Giovanni Panice, Mario Fiore Vitale

Host-Based Pipeline Deployment for the Debezium Platform

summary: The project idea is to provide support for running Debezium on bare metal, virtual machines, and cloud services, using Debezium Server distributions (container images and standalone packages).

Contributor: Divyanshu Kumar

Proposal: link

About the contributor: Divyanshu Kumar is a CSE student and Software Engineer from India focused on high-performance backends and cloud-native systems. A two-time GSoC contributor, C4GT, and SOB participant, he has experience with Java, GWT, and event-driven platforms

Mentors: Mario Fiore Vitale, Giovanni Panice

PyDebeziumAI

summary: The project aims to build an intelligent, Python‑native framework for real‑time reasoning over Change Data Capture (CDC) streams by integrating the capabilities of pydbzengine with modern AI/LLM‑powered Python libraries.

Contributor: Kodukulla Mohnish Mythreya

Proposal: link

About the contributor: Kodukulla Mohnish Mythreya is a 3rd-year CSE student at VIT Chennai and Development Lead at CYSCOM, interested in AI, cloud, developer tooling, and real-time data systems. As a GSoC 2026 contributor with JBoss Community, he’ll work on PyDebeziumAI for real-time CDC reasoning.

Mentors: Jiri Pechanec, Vojtěch Juránek

Debezium Source Connector for Milvus

summary: The project aims to build a Source Connector for Milvus, a vector database designed to power modern AI/ML applications, including semantic search, recommendation systems, RAG (Retrieval‑Augmented Generation), and multimodal search.

Contributor: Kartik Angiras

Proposal: link

About the contributor: Kartik is a tech agnostic developer with an experience in Backend construction, Blockchain engineering and System Design. His open source experience ranges from CDC platforms such as Debezium, Cloud Native projects such as Kyverno, Prometheus Operator, Antrea along with Gemini CLI, Swift etc.

Mentors: Chris Cranford, Giovanni Panice

Debezium Source Connector for Sqlite

summary: The project aims to build a Source Connector for Sqlite, an embedded relational database engine built around a simple architecture where the entire database, including schema, data, and indexes resides in a single cross‑platform file

Contributor: Siddhant Chaturvedi

Proposal: link

About the contributor: Siddhant is a student at IIIT Gwalior with a strong foundation in full-stack development and a passion for system design. He loves exploring backend architecture and large-scale data systems. Away from the keyboard, you will find him swapping his IDE for a camera or a digital canvas.

Mentors: Vincenzo Santonastaso, Giovanni Panice

A Big Thank You to All Applicants

We received many thoughtful proposals and had great discussions with prospective contributors. We want to thank everyone who took the time to learn about Debezium, join the community channels, ask questions, prepare an application and a special thanks to all who submitted any patch as part of getting familiar with Debezium.

If your proposal was not selected this year, we still encourage you to stay involved. GSoC is only one way to contribute to Debezium. The project is open all year round, and we’re always happy to welcome new contributors through issues, documentation improvements, bug fixes, discussions, and feature proposals.

What’s next

We’re looking forward to a productive and exciting summer of open-source collaboration. The selected projects will help expand the Debezium ecosystem and improve the experience for developers working with change data capture. As coding begins, we’ll share updates about the progress of each project and highlight the work our contributors are doing.

Welcome to GSoC 2026 contributors for Debezium, we’re excited to have you with us! 🚀

entry.title: Debezium 3.5.1.Final Released
entry.content:
We’re pleased to announce the release of Debezium 3.5.1.Final, a maintenance release focused on stability, compatibility, and performance improvements across the Debezium platform.

This release brings Informix JDBC driver v15 support, resolves a Debezium Server startup failure, fixes incorrect bytecode generation in the CockroachDB connector, and improves handling of PostgreSQL infinity timestamps in nanosecond precision mode. Additionally, incremental snapshot handling is now more robust when dealing with invalid snapshot parameters.

Let’s take a closer look at the changes included in this release.

  • New features and improvements

  • Other changes

New Features and Improvements

The following covers all new features and improvements, grouped by connector component area.

Debezium Core

Debezium for PostgreSQL

Debezium Server

Debezium for CockroachDB

Debezium for Informix

Debezium Core

More robust incremental snapshot error handling

When an incremental snapshot was triggered with invalid parameters, such as an incorrect surrogate key column, the connector could enter a stuck state where snapshot metadata was persisted to offsets but never cleared. The stop-snapshot signal was ineffective in this scenario, leaving users no option but to manually edit offsets or perform a full connector reset.

Incremental snapshot initialization failures now properly avoid persisting invalid metadata, and the stop-snapshot signal reliably clears snapshot state, making recovery straightforward without manual intervention. (dbz#1533)

Debezium for PostgreSQL

Correct handling of infinity timestamps in nanosecond precision mode

When using time.precision.mode=nanoseconds, PostgreSQL infinity and -infinity timestamp values could overflow and produce negative NanoTimestamp values, leading to incorrect data in downstream consumers. The connector now properly handles these special timestamp values in nanosecond precision mode, ensuring that infinity timestamps are correctly represented without overflow. (dbz#1833)

Debezium Server

Stack overflow startup failure resolved

A stack overflow startup failure has been resolved in Debezium Server when supplying configuration with invalid values. One example that would cause this would be a typo in the connector class name, leading to repeated ClassNotFoundException exceptions. This issue affected Debezium Server 3.5 deployments and prevented the server from starting entirely.

This fix ensures that should there be any startup exceptions due to configuration mistakes, the process reports the error and stops rather than attempting to restart until a stack overflow occurs. (dbz#1779)

Debezium for CockroachDB

Schema caching for improved throughput

The changefeed event processing pipeline now caches parsed Kafka Connect Schema objects per table and reuses them across events when the table schema has not changed. Benchmarks showed the full parsing pipeline previously cost 3-4x raw JSON deserialization due to rebuilding Schema and Struct objects on every event. With schema caching, the common case sees significantly reduced processing overhead, improving overall connector throughput. (dbz#1712)

Debezium for Informix

Support for JDBC driver v15

The Informix connector now supports the Informix JDBC driver v15, which is the official driver for Informix 15 and 14. Previously, the connector only supported JDBC driver v4.50.x, limiting access to new features available in Informix 15. This upgrade ensures compatibility with the latest Informix platform while maintaining support for existing deployments. (dbz#1622)

Other fixes

  • Null value in header converter not handled by ConverterBuilder (dbz#1298)

  • Misleading error message when database connectivity is lost with MySQL 8.4 and later (dbz#1561)

  • Column reselection does not quote all key columns, failing with ORA-00904 (dbz#1750)

  • Improve incremental snapshot documentation with database requirements (dbz#1773)

  • Row archival tests fail for Oracle XStream (dbz#1774)

  • XStream does not decode all XML encodings (dbz#1775)

  • Redis sink hangs when using Redis Cluster (dbz#1793)

  • LogFileNotFoundException due to archive log deduplication ignoring redo thread in Oracle RAC (dbz#1801)

  • Compatibility issues with Informix Changestream Client v1.1.4 (dbz#1802)

  • Compatibility issues with Informix JDBC driver v15.0.1.1 (dbz#1803)

  • ByLogicalTableRouter materializes schema defaults for nullable fields, overwriting real NULL values (dbz#1848)

  • SQL Server tests have started to time out (dbz#1852)

  • Connector fails to restart with trust_greater_lsn after non-captured table updates (dbz#1863)

  • Connector stuck after connection idle-killed during schema history recovery (dbz#1877)

  • Dead documentation links in Quarkus extension (dbz#1883)

  • Fix for copy completed sequence event and null last primary key (dbz#1887)

  • Connector pom.xml uses wrong Java target property, producing Java 21 bytecode instead of Java 17 (dbz#1922)

  • IllegalArgumentException when CDC capture polling interval is 0 (dbz#1923)

In total, 23 issues were resolved in Debezium 3.5.1.Final. The list of changes can also be found in our release notes.

A big thank you to all the contributors from the community who worked diligently on this release:

entry.title: Join the Debezium Community Weekly Forum

link.title: Join the Debezium Community Weekly Forum

entry.content:
The Debezium community grows through open collaboration among users, contributors, maintainers, and the wider data-streaming ecosystem.

Starting Tuesday, May 19, we are opening our weekly team meeting on every Tuesday to the broader Debezium community. Whether you are a contributor, evaluating Debezium, or simply interested in change data capture and streaming, you are welcome to attend.

The meeting duration is scheduled for 45 minutes. However, to respect everyone’s time, meetings may conclude earlier if the agenda is completed and there are no extra topic for discussion. The minimum meeting duration will be 15 minutes.

Meeting Agenda and Participation

To keep the meetings transparent and collaborative, the agenda is maintained in a shared Google Document that is open for external comments and suggestions.

You can view the agenda document here:

Debezium Community Meeting Agenda

Community members are encouraged to propose topics, discussion items, demos, questions, or updates ahead of the meeting.

New discussion topics should first be proposed on Zulip, so the maintainers can help shape the discussion and decide whether it should be added to an upcoming meeting agenda.

Request to add a topic to the agenda via Zulip:

Debezium Forum Agenda

Calendar and Scheduling

Debezium community meetings and events are listed in our shared Google Calendar. You can browse the schedule online or subscribe to the public iCalendar feed to keep upcoming events in your own calendar application.

Public calendar:

Debezium Community Calendar

We hope these meetings provide another accessible way for the community to collaborate, exchange ideas, discuss roadmap items, highlight ongoing work, and help shape the future of Debezium together.

We look forward to seeing you there!
